1.pericope_label: And seeing the multitudes, he went up into a mountain: and when he was set, his disciples came unto him: And he opened his mouth, and taught them, saying,

schools.summary: Ellicott opens with the standing of the discourse. Matthew, who appears in the earliest traditions as a collector of our Lord's oracles, places it in the forefront of his record as a great pattern discourse, that which more than any other represented the teaching with which the work began; it impressed itself on the minds of men in the first age of the church more than any other part of the record, being quoted by James and Barnabas and Clement of Rome and Ignatius and Polycarp, and in recent time has drawn the admiring reverence even of many who do not look on the Preacher as the faith of Christendom looks on him. Two preliminary questions he raises. Whether this is the verbatim report of one discourse he treats as genuinely open: much of it recurs scattered through Luke, where the same sayings come as the answer to a question or the rebuke of a special fault, and one might think the two Evangelists had come across a collection of our Lord's words and used it each after his own manner, Matthew dovetailing them into a continuous whole and Luke tracing them to their sources. Against that he sets the evidence of a systematic plan in the first two chapters: the Beatitudes and the verses that follow set forth the conditions of blessedness and the ideal life of the kingdom; then comes the contrast between the righteousness required for it and that which passed current among the scribes, carried through their way of dealing with the commandments and through the three great elements of the religious life, almsgiving, prayer and fasting; then warnings against the love of money and its cares. The Sermon as it stands might have been spoken in thirty or forty minutes, and there is no reason to think that the necessary limit of our Lord's discourses; assume something longer, heard by a multitude with no one taking notes, and many trying years afterwards to record what they remembered, and then a writer collecting those scattered members, comparing what others had written with what he recalled, and setting them in order, and the natural outcome is what we find. He concludes for substantially the report of a single discourse with possibly a few additions, the first full proclamation of the perfect law of liberty, and warns against making it the limit of theology, since our Lord spoke the word as men were able to hear it and this was the beginning and not the end of the training of his disciples. On the identity with Luke's sermon he holds the two quite distinct, each with a traceable purpose and method of its own. Barnes is less decided, thinking it not improbable that the substance was repeated on different occasions and to different people, with parts omitted, and that Luke recorded it as pronounced on one of those. On the setting Barnes places the hill somewhere near Capernaum, notes the eminence shown by tradition to the northwest of the ancient site and called on maps the Mount of Beatitudes, and allows there is no positive evidence for it; the ascent he explains simply, as more convenient for addressing a multitude than the same level with them, and sitting as the common mode of teaching among the Jews. Robertson is exact about the article: it is the mountain and not a mountain, the one there where Jesus and the crowds were, and the Greek article is poorly handled in most English versions. He reconciles the three Gospels by letting all three purposes stand, that he went up to get in closer contact with the disciples, that he went out into the mountain to pray, and that he went up and called the twelve; and he finds no real difficulty in taking the Sermon on the Mount and the Sermon on the Plain as one and the same, since Luke has him come down after a night of prayer to a level place on the mountain. The teaching he reads as an inchoative imperfect, that he began to teach, sitting on the mountain side as the rabbis did instead of standing, and opening his mouth wide to speak loud enough for the great throng.

Calvin dismisses the question of identity in a sentence: those who think this sermon different from the one in Luke rest their opinion on a very light and frivolous argument, since it is a mistake to read Luke's words about the plain as immediately connected with the statement that he spoke thus. The design of both Evangelists was to collect into one place the leading points of the doctrine of Christ which related to a devout and holy life; Luke passes from miracles to doctrine without pointing out either time or place, and Matthew takes no notice of the time but only mentions the place. He thinks it probable that the discourse was not delivered until the twelve had been chosen, but declines to be too precise about an order of time which he saw the Spirit of God had disregarded, and asks only that pious and modest readers be satisfied with a brief summary of Christ's doctrine collected out of his many and various discourses. The ascent he refuses to allegorise: he will not have the ingenious speculation of those who make the mountain a lesson in elevating the mind above worldly cares, since the design was rather to seek a retreat where he might obtain relaxation for himself and his disciples at a distance from the multitude. The opening of the mouth he calls a redundancy of expression partaking of the Hebrew idiom, faulty in other languages but frequent among the Hebrews; many take it as an emphatic mode of expression drawing attention to something remarkable, but as some passages of Scripture countenance an opposite view he prefers the plainer exposition. He then states why the discourse begins where it does: not only the great body of the people but even the learned hold the error that the happy man is the one free from annoyance who attains all his wishes and leads a joyful and easy life, happiness being generally estimated from the present state. Christ therefore, in order to accustom his own people to bear the cross, exposes that mistaken opinion; for it is impossible that men should mildly bend the neck to bear calamities and reproaches so long as they think patience at variance with a happy life, and the only consolation that sweetens the bitterness of the cross is the conviction that we are happy in the midst of miseries. This doctrine he acknowledges to be widely removed from the common opinion, but the disciples of Christ must learn the philosophy of placing their happiness beyond the world and above the affections of the flesh.

Clarke gives the chapter's argument in brief and then fills in the circumstances. The month and season he works out: the Israelites seem to have left Babylon in spring, which is to say that he reckons by the plain course of events rather than by any reported date, and so here he reckons the crowds of the preceding chapter to be the multitudes meant, which should have made the first verse of this one. The ascent he explains by audibility, that he went up to have the greater advantage of speaking so as to be heard by the great concourse which followed him, and he thinks it very probable that nothing more is meant than a small hill or eminence, since on a high mountain they could not have heard and at a great distance he would not have sat down. Sitting he calls the usual posture of public teachers among the Jews and among many other people, so much so that sitting became a synonymous term for teaching among the rabbis. The word disciple he glosses literally as scholar: those who originally followed Christ considered him in the light of a divine teacher, and conscious of their ignorance and the importance of his teaching put themselves under his tuition that they might be instructed in heavenly things; having been taught the mysteries of the kingdom they became closely attached to their divine Master, imitating his life and manners and recommending his salvation to all the circle of their acquaintance, which he says is still the characteristic of a genuine disciple. Wesley adds that the multitudes were seen at some distance as they came from every quarter, that the mountain was near and had room for them all, and that the disciples addressed were not the twelve only but all who desired to learn of him. The opening of the mouth he takes as a phrase which always denotes a set and solemn discourse, and he reads the whole as the complete art of happiness: to bless men, to make men happy, was the great business for which our Lord came into the world, and accordingly he here pronounces eight blessings together, annexing them to so many steps in Christianity. Knowing that happiness is our common aim, and that an innate instinct continually urges us to pursue it, he applies in the kindest manner to that instinct and directs it to its proper object, since though all men desire happiness few attain it because they seek it where it is not to be found. Wesley bids us observe the benevolent condescension of our Lord, who seems as it were to lay aside his supreme authority as our legislator that he may the better act the part of our friend and Saviour, and instead of the lofty style of positive commands insinuates his will and our duty in a more gentle and engaging way, by pronouncing those happy who comply with it.

Henry takes the sermon's parts in order, the Preacher, the place, the auditors and the solemnity. The Preacher is the Prince of preachers, the great Prophet of his church, who came into the world to be the Light of the world; the prophets and John had done virtuously in preaching, but Christ excelled them all, being the eternal Wisdom that lay in the bosom of the Father and the eternal Word by whom God has in these last days spoken to us. The miraculous cures of the preceding chapter he reads as intended to make way for this sermon and to dispose people to receive instruction from one in whom there appeared so much of a divine power and goodness, and he thinks the discourse was probably the summary or rehearsal of what Christ had preached up and down in the synagogues of Galilee; his text was that the kingdom of heaven is at hand, and this sermon expounds the former part of it, showing what it is to repent, which is to reform both in judgment and practice. The place he makes part of the meaning. In this as in other things our Lord was but ill accommodated, having no convenient place to preach in any more than to lay his head on: while the scribes and Pharisees had Moses' chair to sit in with all possible ease and honour and state, and there corrupted the law, the great Teacher of truth is driven out to the desert and finds no better pulpit than a mountain can afford, and not one of the holy mountains either, but a common mountain, by which Christ would intimate that there is no such distinguishing holiness of places now under the gospel as there was under the law, and that it is the will of God that men should pray and preach everywhere. He preached on a mountain because upon a mountain the law was given, and this was a solemn promulgation of the Christian law; but Henry marks the difference, that when the law was given the Lord came down upon the mountain and now the Lord went up, that then he spoke in thunder and lightning and now in a still small voice, that then the people were ordered to keep their distance and now they are invited to draw near, which he calls a blessed change. The auditors were the disciples, who came at his call, and to them he directed his speech because they followed him for love and learning while others attended him only for cures, because they were willing to be taught, because they would understand what to others was foolishness, and because they were to teach others; yet it was in the hearing of the multitude, no bounds being set about this mountain to keep the people off as they were about Sinai, since through Christ we have access to God not only to speak to him but to hear from him. The solemnity is in the words when he was set: Christ preached many times occasionally and by interlocutory discourses, but this was a set sermon, and he sat down as a Judge or Lawgiver, which intimates with what sedateness and composure the things of God should be spoken and heard. The opening of the mouth Henry takes for a Hebrew periphrasis of speaking, though some find in it the solemnity of a voice raised for a large congregation; he had long spoken by his servants the prophets and opened their mouths, but now he opened his own and spoke with freedom, as one having authority.

debates: Whether this is the same discourse Luke reports, where Ellicott holds the two quite distinct, each with a traceable purpose and method of its own, Calvin calls the opinion that they differ a very light and frivolous argument resting on nothing but a misreading of how Luke's words connect, Robertson finds no real difficulty in taking them as one and reconciles the settings from Luke's own account of the descent to a level place on the mountain, and Barnes leaves it open, thinking the substance not improbably repeated on different occasions with parts omitted.

Why he went up into the mountain, where Clarke and Barnes answer from audibility and convenience, Clarke adding that nothing more than a small hill can be meant since on a high mountain he could not have been heard, Robertson has him go up for closer contact with the disciples and lets Luke's prayer and Mark's calling of the twelve stand alongside it, Calvin expressly dismisses the allegory of minds lifted above worldly cares and makes it a retreat from the crowd, and Henry makes the common mountain itself a lesson, set against Sinai.

What the opening of the mouth signifies, where Calvin calls it a redundancy after the Hebrew idiom and prefers that plain account to the emphatic one, Henry takes it for a Hebrew periphrasis of speaking while allowing that some find solemnity in it, and Wesley holds that the phrase always denotes a set and solemn discourse, with Robertson hearing in it a voice raised loud enough for the throng.
outliers: Ellicott reckons that the Sermon as it stands might have been spoken in thirty or forty minutes, and reconstructs its transmission from hearers who took no notes and recorded years afterwards what they remembered.
Robertson insists on the Greek article, the mountain and not a mountain, and reads the teaching as an inchoative imperfect, that he began to teach.

3.pericope_label: Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted. Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth. Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled. Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy. Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God. Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God. Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness’ sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake. Rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven: for so persecuted they the prophets which were before you.

schools.summary: Ellicott begins with the word itself, which differs from the one used later in this Gospel in expressing a permanent state of felicity rather than the passive reception of a blessing bestowed by another. On the poor in spirit he says the limitation, as in the pure in heart, points to the region of life in which the poverty is found; Luke has no such qualifying clause and there the words speak of outward poverty as in itself a less perilous and therefore happier state than that of riches, while here the blessedness belongs to those who, whatever their outward state, are in their inward life as men who feel they have nothing of their own and must be receivers before they give. The mourning he distinguishes from the sorrow of the world that works death: it is the mourning over sin itself and the stain it has left on the soul, and the promise is of the special comfort, counsel included, which the mourner needs. On meekness he thinks the word was used in its popular meaning without reference to the definitions of ethical writers, but recalls Aristotle's account of the character of one who has the passion of resentment under control and is therefore tranquil and untroubled, as partly determining that popular use. The hunger and thirst he hears as the lesson learnt from the recent experience of the wilderness, the craving of bodily hunger become a parable of the higher yearning, and notes that desires after earthly goods are frustrated or end in satiety while to this only belongs the promise of being filled. On the pure in heart he is careful that the noun determines the region in which the purity is found, the heart representing desires and affections as the spirit represents the will, and that the purity meant is neither the outward and ceremonial ideal of the Pharisee nor, as Christian language too often limits it, the absence of one special form of sensual sin, but the exclusion of every element of baseness, the impurity of hate or greed of gain no less than that of lust. The peacemakers he distinguishes from the merely peaceable, this being the higher form of the same grace acting energetically upon others, and he finds a profound significance in the order, that the beatitude rightly follows the pure in heart since it is the absence of all baseness that gives the power to make peace, and that the persecution beatitude follows the peacemakers because their work is not light and easy. The last promise he notes is the same as the first, so that we end as we began with the kingdom of heaven. In the change to the second person he hears the beatitude uttered for the first time not as a general law but as the portion of the listening disciples, and he finds three forms of suffering in it, the vague contempt showing itself in gibes and nicknames, persecution generally, and deliberate calumnies such as those of the foul banquets spread against believers in the first two centuries. The word falsely he reports absent from the best manuscripts, probably added as a safeguard against the thought that a man might claim the reward of the persecuted while really guilty of the crimes laid against him; and on the reward he holds that even here it is not of debt but of grace, the temper to which it is promised practically excluding any claim as of right. Barnes glosses blessed as happy, referring to whatever produces felicity from whatever quarter it may come, and reports the dispute over the poor, whether the poor in reference to the things of this life or the humble are meant, noting that the gospel is said to be preached to the poor and that such persons have peculiar facilities for being saved, while riches produce care and anxiety and the danger of losing heaven; to be poor in spirit he settles as having a humble opinion of ourselves. The mourning he likewise finds capable of two meanings, affliction by the loss of friends or possessions, or mourning over sin, and since Christ came to preach repentance he thinks the latter particularly in view, adding that the gospel only can give true comfort in affliction, other sources blunting the sensibilities or producing a sullen submission without pointing to the true source of comfort. Meekness he defines sharply as patience in the reception of injuries, neither meanness nor a surrender of our rights nor cowardice, but the opposite of sudden anger, of malice and of long-harboured vengeance; and he instances Christ insisting on his right before the officer who struck him and Paul insisting on his before the magistrates at Philippi, both of them models of meekness who bore much patiently without being passionate. Hunger and thirst he takes for strong desire, no wants being so keen or so imperiously demanding supply, and instances those shipwrecked and doomed to wander over burning sands. The peacemakers he describes practically, as those who use their influence to reconcile opposing parties and prevent lawsuits and hostilities in families and neighbourhoods, and says no man is more like God than he who does it, that friends and neighbours and men of influence and lawyers and physicians may do much to promote peace, and that it should be taken in hand at the beginning, since the beginning of strife is like the letting out of water. On persecution he warns that we are not to seek it nor provoke it by strange sentiments or conduct or by modes of speech unnecessarily offensive, but that if others persecute us in the honest effort to be Christians we are to count it a blessing; and he lays an emphasis on falsely, since it is not blessed to have evil spoken of us if we deserve it. The reward of such suffering he says is great, which is why the crown of martyrdom has been thought the brightest, and why many of the early Christians sought to become martyrs and threw themselves in the way of their persecutors, literally rejoicing and leaping for joy at the prospect of death.

Calvin reads the first beatitude against the common exposition. Luke gives nothing more than a simple metaphor, but as the poverty of many is accursed and unhappy Matthew expresses more clearly the intention of Christ: many are pressed down by distresses and yet continue to swell inwardly with pride and cruelty, while Christ pronounces happy those who, chastened and subdued by afflictions, submit themselves wholly to God and with inward humility betake themselves to him for protection. Others, he notes, explain the poor in spirit as those who claim nothing for themselves and are so emptied of confidence in the flesh that they acknowledge their poverty; but since the words of Luke and those of Matthew must have the same meaning, he has no doubt the appellation is given to those who are pressed and afflicted by adversity, the only difference being that Matthew, by adding an epithet, confines the happiness to those who under the discipline of the cross have learned to be humble. The second beatitude he calls an appendage and confirmation of the first: the ordinary belief is that calamities render a man unhappy, and nothing is supposed more inconsistent with happiness than mourning, but Christ does not merely affirm that mourners are not unhappy, he shows that their very mourning contributes to a happy life by preparing them to receive eternal joy and furnishing them with motives to seek true happiness in God alone. On meekness he admits the promise might seem exceedingly foolish, since those who warmly repel attacks and whose hand is ever ready to revenge injuries are rather the men who claim the dominion of the earth, and experience shows that the more mildly wickedness is endured the bolder it becomes, whence the diabolical proverb that we must howl with the wolves because the wolves will devour whoever makes himself a sheep; but Christ sets his own protection and the Father's against the fury of wicked men. The hunger and thirst he takes figuratively, a part put for the whole: to hunger and thirst means to suffer poverty, to want the necessaries of life, and even to be defrauded of one's right, and Matthew by naming righteousness makes one class stand for all the rest and represents the unworthy treatment more strongly, since though they groan they desire nothing but what is proper. The merciful he calls another paradox contradicting the judgment of men, the world reckoning happy those who give themselves no concern about the distresses of others and consult their own ease, while Christ pronounces happy those prepared not only to endure their own afflictions but to take a share in the afflictions of others and to clothe themselves as it were with the same affections. On purity of heart he observes that though simplicity is universally acknowledged to be the mother of all virtues, hardly one person in a hundred does not put craftiness in the place of the greatest virtue, so that those are commonly accounted happy whose ingenuity is exercised in the successful practice of deceit; Christ does not at all agree with carnal reason when he pronounces happy those who take no delight in cunning but converse sincerely and express nothing by word or look which they do not feel in their heart. The peacemakers he defines as those who not only seek peace and avoid quarrels but labour to settle differences among others, and he explains the promise by the cost of the work: since reconciling those at variance is laborious and irksome, men of a mild disposition are compelled to endure the indignity of hearing reproaches and complaints on all sides, because every one would desire advocates to defend his own cause, and so Christ bids us look up to the judgment of his Father rather than depend on the favour of men. The persecution clause he says the disciples have very great need of, and the harder it is for the flesh to admit the more earnestly it should be meditated: we cannot be Christ's soldiers on any other condition than to have the greater part of the world rising in hostility against us and pursuing us even to death, since Satan will never cease to fill his followers with rage against the members of Christ; it is monstrous and unnatural that men who study to live righteously should be tormented as they do not deserve. The reviling he reads as comfort, lest believers lose courage when they see themselves detestable in the eyes of the world, for to be thrown out of the church as ungodly and profane was no light temptation, and Christ knew there is no class of men more envenomed than hypocrites; from which Calvin concludes how little reason there is to dread the excommunication of those tyrants who banish us from their synagogues because we are unwilling to renounce Christ. On the reward he refutes the notion of merit directly: there is no mutual relation between the reward and merit, the promise being free, and if we consider the imperfections and faults of any good works done by the very best of men there is no work God can judge worthy of reward; and he adds the caution that a man who suffers persecution for his own fault must not forthwith boast himself a martyr of Christ, as the Donatists of old were pleased with themselves on the single ground that the magistrates were against them. Gill rules out the merely poor at once: not the poor in purse, or who are so with respect to things temporal, for though God has chosen and called many in such a condition of life he has not called all, and the kingdom of heaven cannot be said to belong to them all or only; it is the spiritually poor who are meant, and all mankind is spiritually poor, having nothing fit to eat and no clothes. The mourning he makes particular and daily: for the sin of their nature, for indwelling sin which is always working and is a continual grief of mind, for the unbelief of their hearts notwithstanding the many promises and discoveries of grace, and for their daily infirmities and many sins of life, because these are committed against a God of love and grace and grieve the Spirit and dishonour the gospel. The meek he describes at length as those not easily provoked to anger, who patiently bear injuries and affronts, carry themselves courteously and affably to all, have the meanest thoughts of themselves and the best of others, do not envy the gifts and graces of other men, are willing to be instructed and admonished by the meanest of the saints, and quietly submit to the will of God in adverse dispensations of providence. The merciful he divides between the bodies and the souls of men, showing mercy to the poor and indigent by sympathising with them and distributing to them, not only using expressions of pity but communicating with readiness and cheerfulness and with a view to the glory of God, and showing mercy to souls by instructing the ignorant. Purity he locates precisely: not in the head, for men may have pure notions and impure hearts; not in the hand or in outward conversation only, as the Pharisees were outwardly righteous before men while inwardly full of impurity; but in the heart, which is naturally unclean and which it is not in man's power to make clean. The peacemakers he distinguishes from any human mediator between God and man, since no man can make his own peace with God and Christ in that sense is the only peacemaker; these are peacemakers between men and men, being of peaceable dispositions themselves and living peaceably with all. The reviling he reads as prophetic of what the first Christians in particular were to endure for Christ's sake, men branding them with infamy and loading them with disgrace, and the rejoicing as grounded both in the honour put upon them and in the glory that shall follow their sufferings.

Clarke takes the word for happy to its root, deriving it from a privative and a word for fate or death, so that the person Christ terms happy is one not under the influence of fate or chance but governed by an all-wise providence, having every step directed to the attainment of immortal glory; he supports the sense from Homer, who calls the supreme gods the ever happy and immortal and opposes them to mortal men. The mourners are those who, feeling their spiritual poverty, mourn after God and lament the iniquity that separated them from the fountain of blessedness: every one flies from sorrow and seeks after joy, yet true joy must necessarily be the fruit of sorrow, and only such persons as are deeply convinced of the sinfulness of sin, who feel the plague of their own heart and turn with disgust from all worldly consolations because of their insufficiency, have God's promise of solid comfort; the comforting he glosses from the Greek as a calling near, since he will call them to himself and speak the words of pardon and peace and life eternal to their hearts. The meek he derives from a word meaning easy, those of a quiet gentle spirit in opposition to the proud and supercilious scribes and Pharisees and their disciples, and he notes that the English compound gentleman once fully expressed the meaning of the original though it has now almost wholly lost that signification; his etymology makes the meek man a companion or equal, ever ready to associate with the meanest of those who fear God, feeling himself superior to none and well knowing that he has nothing of spiritual or temporal good but what he has received from the mere bounty of God. The hunger and thirst he presses as a natural appetite of the soul answering to the body's: as the body depends for nourishment and health and strength upon the earth, so the soul depends upon heaven, and heavenly things cannot support the body nor earthly things the soul, each being unsuited to the other's nature; when the uneasy sensation of hunger takes place in the stomach we know we must get food or perish, and when the soul is awakened to a sense of its wants and begins to hunger after righteousness we know it must be purified by the Holy Spirit. Mercy he traces through two languages: among the Jews the word signified both the pardon of injuries and almsgiving, and our Lord undoubtedly takes it in its fullest latitude; the Latin from which our word derives is composed of pitying and the heart, so that mercy supposes two things, a distressed object and a disposition of the heart which is affected at the sight of such an object, and the virtue is no other than a lively emotion of the heart excited by the discovery of a creature's misery, manifesting itself outwardly by effects suited to its nature. Purity of heart he sets against the Pharisees, who affected outward purity while their hearts were full of corruption and defilement, a principal part of the Jewish religion consisting in outward washings and cleansings on the ground of which they expected to see God; he cites Origen against Celsus, that God has no body and is therefore invisible, but men of contemplation can discern him with the heart and understanding, while a defiled heart cannot see God. Peace he derives from a word for connecting into one, since as war distracts and divides nations and families and individuals from each other, inducing them to pursue different objects and different interests, so peace restores them to a state of unity, giving them one object and one interest; a peacemaker is a man who, being endowed with a generous public spirit, labours for the public good and feels his own interest promoted in promoting that of others, and therefore instead of fanning the fire of strife uses his influence and wisdom to reconcile the contending parties, which is why the gospel is called the gospel of peace. Persecution he glosses as being hard pressed upon and pursued with repeated acts of enmity, and admits the saying sounds strange, that they are happy who suffer, and stranger still that the righteous should suffer merely because they are such; but such is the enmity of the human heart to everything of God and goodness that all who live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution in one form or other, since as the religion of Christ gives no quarter to vice, so the vicious will give no quarter to this religion or to its professors. The reviling he distinguishes from the persecution of the preceding verse, that comprehending all outward acts of violence, all that the hand can do, and this all calumny and slander, all that the tongue can effect; but since the verb rendered persecute is a forensic term signifying legal persecutions and public accusations, which though totally unsubstantiated were the means of destroying multitudes of the primitive Christians, he thinks our Lord probably refers to such, and he cannot think without horror of the great numbers burnt alive in England on such accusations under the reign of Queen Mary. The rejoicing he grounds in the testimony of a good conscience, without which suffering has nothing but misery in it, and he notes that leaping for joy was literally done by the martyrs in Mary's days; the great reward he parallels from a Talmudical tract, that the day is short and the work great and the labourers slow and the reward great and the father of the family urgent, and he concludes that since God gives the grace to suffer and then crowns that grace with glory, the reward is plainly not of debt but of grace. Wesley sets out the plan of the whole discourse, a sweet invitation to true holiness and happiness, a persuasive to impart it to others, a description of true Christian holiness in which the latter part exactly answers the former, and a conclusion giving a sure mark of the true way, warning against false prophets and exhorting to follow after holiness. The mourners he takes either for their own sins or for other men's, and as steadily and habitually serious, to be comforted more solidly and deeply even in this world and eternally in heaven. The meek are those who hold all their passions and affections evenly balanced, and shall have all things really necessary for life and godliness, enjoying whatever portion God has given them here and hereafter possessing the new earth wherein dwells righteousness. Those who hunger and thirst after righteousness hunger after the holiness here described and shall be satisfied with it; the merciful are the tender-hearted who love all men as themselves, and whatever mercy we desire from God we are to show to our brethren; the pure in heart are the sanctified who love God with all their hearts, and shall see God in all things here and hereafter in glory; the peacemakers are those who out of love to God and man do all possible good to all men, peace in the scripture sense implying all blessings temporal and eternal, and they shall be acknowledged children of God by God and man. One would imagine, he adds, that a person of this amiable temper and behaviour would be the darling of mankind, but our Lord well knew it would not be so as long as Satan was the prince of this world, and therefore warns them beforehand. Persecution for righteousness' sake he defines as suffering because men have or follow after the righteousness here described, and he holds that the righteous man, the mourner, the pure in heart, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer it, the world always saying, away with such fellows from the earth, since they are made to reprove our thoughts and their lives are not like other men's. The reward he takes as even over and above the happiness that naturally and directly results from holiness.

Henry observes that Christ begins his sermon with blessings, for he came into the world to bless us, and does it as one having authority, as one that can command the blessing; his pronouncing them happy makes them so, for those whom he blesses are blessed indeed. The Old Testament ended with a curse and the gospel begins with a blessing, and he compares the two mountains from which the blessings and cursings of the law were read: there the curses are expressed and the blessings only implied, here the blessings are expressed and the curses implied, and in both life and death are set before us, but the law appeared more as a ministration of death to deter us from sin and the gospel as a dispensation of life to allure us to Christ. Each blessing he says has a double intention, to show who are to be accounted truly happy and what their characters are, and wherein true happiness consists. The design is fourfold: to rectify the ruinous mistakes of a blind and carnal world, whose general opinion is that the rich and great and honourable are the blessed, and to give us quite another notion of blessedness which, however paradoxical it appears to the prejudiced, is a doctrine of eternal truth by which we must shortly be judged; to remove the discouragements of the weak and poor who receive the gospel, by assuring them that it does not make happy only those eminent in gifts and graces and usefulness, but that even the least in the kingdom whose heart is upright with God is happy in its honours and privileges; to invite souls to Christ and make way for his law into their hearts, the blessings coming at the beginning to prepare the hearers rather than at the end to dismiss them; and to settle and sum up the articles of agreement between God and man, since the scope of the divine revelation is to let us know what God expects from us and what we may then expect from him. He notes that some of the wiser heathen had notions of blessedness looking towards this, and quotes Seneca's description of the blessed man as only the honest good man, whom no occurrences elate or deject, whose true pleasure consists in a contempt of pleasure, and to whom the only good is virtue and the only evil vice. Poverty of spirit he distinguishes from the poor-spiritedness that is a sin and a snare, cowardice and base fear and a willing subjection to the lusts of men; this is a gracious disposition of soul by which we are emptied of self in order to our being filled with Jesus Christ, and he gives it three parts, to be contentedly poor and bring our mind to our condition when it is a low condition, to be humble and lowly in our own eyes and think meanly of what we are and have and do, and to come off from all confidence in our own righteousness and strength that we may depend only on the merit of Christ for justification and his Spirit for sanctification. He puts it first among the Christian graces, noting that the philosophers did not reckon humility among their moral virtues but Christ puts it first, since self-denial is the first lesson in his school and the foundation of all other graces is laid in humility: those who would build high must begin low. The mourners he calls another strange blessing fitly following the former, since the poor are accustomed to mourn and the graciously poor mourn graciously; we are apt to think blessed are the merry, but Christ, who was himself a great mourner, says blessed are the mourners. He distinguishes a sinful mourning which is an enemy to blessedness, the sorrow of the world, from a natural mourning which may prove a friend to blessedness by the grace of God working with it, and from the gracious mourning that qualifies for blessedness, which is both a penitential mourning for our own sins and a sympathising mourning for the afflictions of others. Heaven he says will be a heaven indeed to those who go mourning thither, a harvest of joy returning a seed-time of tears, a mountain of joy to which our way lies through a vale of tears. The meek are those who quietly submit themselves to God, to his word and to his rod, and are gentle towards all men, who can bear provocation without being inflamed by it, are either silent or return a soft answer, can be cool when others are hot, and in their patience keep possession of their own souls when they can scarcely keep possession of anything else; they are rarely and hardly provoked but quickly and easily pacified, and would rather forgive twenty injuries than revenge one. Their inheriting the earth he notes is quoted from the Psalms and is almost the only express temporal promise in all the New Testament, not that they shall always have much of the earth, much less be put off with that only, but that this branch of godliness has in a special manner the promise of the life that now is, meekness having a real tendency to promote our health and wealth and comfort and safety even in this world. On the hunger and thirst he reports both readings: some understand it of outward poverty and a low condition which makes it vain for men to seek justice, so that they hunger and thirst after it but cannot have it because of the power on the side of their oppressors; and he grants that such are blessed if they suffer with a good conscience and refer themselves to God to plead their cause. But he holds it certainly to be understood spiritually, righteousness standing for all spiritual blessings, which we must truly and really desire as one hungry and thirsty desires meat and drink, with desires earnest and importunate, and which, since hunger and thirst are appetites that return frequently, rest not in anything attained but are carried out towards renewed pardons and daily fresh supplies of grace. The merciful are those piously and charitably inclined to pity and help and succour persons in misery; a man may be truly merciful who has not wherewithal to be bountiful, and then God accepts the willing mind. Purity of heart he calls the most comprehensive of all the beatitudes, where holiness and happiness are fully described and put together, the heart being required pure in opposition to mixture and pure in opposition to pollution, as wine unmixed and water unmuddied; and the seeing of God he calls the perfection of the soul's happiness, promised to the pure only, since none but the pure are capable of seeing God, nor would it be a felicity to the impure, for as he cannot endure to look upon their iniquity so they cannot endure to look upon his purity. The peacemakers have a peaceable disposition and a peaceable conversation, industriously preserving the peace that it be not broken and recovering it when it is broken, being repairers of the breaches; and he allows that the making of peace is sometimes a thankless office, since it is the lot of him who parts a fray to have blows on both sides, but it is a good office and we must be forward to it. From this beatitude he draws a conclusion about method: since the peacemakers are blessed, woe to the peace-breakers, and by this it appears that Christ never intended to have his religion propagated by fire and sword or penal laws, or to acknowledge bigotry or intemperate zeal as the mark of his disciples. The last beatitude he calls the greatest paradox of all and peculiar to Christianity, and therefore put last and more largely insisted upon, doubled like Pharaoh's dream because it is hardly credited. He describes the case of suffering saints at length, hunted and pursued as noxious beasts, reviled and nicknamed, with all manner of evil said against them falsely, and notes that reviling the saints is persecuting them and will be found so shortly; that it is for righteousness' sake, which precludes from the blessedness those who suffer justly and are evil spoken of truly for real crimes, since it is not the suffering but the cause that makes the martyr; and that though there is nothing in such sufferings that can in strictness merit of God, the reward in heaven is so great as far to transcend the service, and well secured out of the reach of chance and fraud and violence. The prophets who went before, he adds, were persecuted in like manner, and it is a comfort to see the way of suffering a beaten road and an honour to follow such leaders.

debates: What the poverty of spirit is, where Gill rules out the poor in purse outright since God has called many in that condition but not all, Ellicott makes the qualifying clause point to the region of life in which the poverty is found and notes that Luke, lacking it, speaks of outward poverty, Barnes reports the dispute and settles for a humble opinion of ourselves, Henry defines it as being emptied of self in order to be filled with Christ, and Calvin dissents from them all, holding that since Luke and Matthew must mean the same thing the name belongs to those pressed and afflicted by adversity, the added epithet confining the happiness to those who under the discipline of the cross have learned to be humble.

What the hunger and thirst after righteousness is, where Calvin takes it as a part put for the whole and makes it mean suffering poverty, wanting the necessaries of life and being defrauded of one's right, Henry reports that reading of oppressed men denied justice and allows them the blessing but holds the spiritual sense certain, and Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott take the craving for righteousness alone, Clarke pressing the analogy of the body's appetites and Ellicott hearing the lesson of the wilderness in it.

Whether the words without a cause belong to the text of the reviling clause, and more broadly whether falsely does, where Ellicott reports the word absent from the best manuscripts and probably added as a safeguard against a man claiming the reward while really guilty, while Barnes lays a positive emphasis on it, since it is not blessed to have evil spoken of us if we deserve it, and Calvin adds the caution that one who suffers for his own fault must not boast himself a martyr, as the Donatists were pleased with themselves because the magistrates were against them.
outliers: Clarke derives the word for happy from a root meaning not subject to fate, and supports the sense from Homer's epithet for the ever happy and immortal gods.

Henry quotes Seneca's description of the blessed man, whom no occurrences elate or deject and whose true pleasure consists in a contempt of pleasure, as one of the heathen notions looking towards this teaching.
themes: Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted.
Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth.
Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled.
Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy.
Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.
Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.
Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness’ sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake.
Rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven: for so persecuted they the prophets which were before you.

13.pericope_label: Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men. Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid. Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house. Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.

schools.summary: Ellicott speaks of the disciples here in their ideal character, as the germ of a new Israel called to a prophetic work, preserving the earth from moral putrescence and decay; the general reference to the antiseptic action of salt he thinks enough to give an adequate meaning to the words, but the special reference to the sacrificial use of salt elsewhere makes it probable enough that there was some allusion to that thought also. On the salt that has lost its savour he is careful with the evidence: the salt commonly used by the Jews of old came from the hill by the Dead Sea and was known as the Salt of Sodom, and the eastern traveller Maundrell reports finding lumps of rock-salt there which had become partially flavourless, but Ellicott adds that he is not aware of this having been confirmed by recent observation. The light of the world he reserves in its highest or truest sense to Christ and to him only, the comparison to the lamp in the following verse showing that even here the disciples are spoken of as shining with a derived brightness flowing to them from the Fount of light. For the city set on a hill he suggests, on the assumption that the Sermon was preached from one of the hills of Galilee, that our Lord may have looked or pointed at Safed, high above the sea and commanding one of the grandest panoramic views in Palestine, now one of the four holy cities of the Jews and probably existing as a fortress in our Lord's time; though he allows the imagery might instead come from the prophetic visions of the Zion of the future. The lamp he distinguishes from a candle in the common meaning of the word, a portable vessel supplied with oil, applied apparently to the cheaper vessels of the poor rather than those of the wealthy, and not the same word as that used for the lamps of the wise and foolish virgins; Wiclif, he notes, translates it lantern. The presence of the article in the Greek, under the bushel and on the lamp-stand, he takes to imply the familiarity of the objects, each cottage having one such article of furniture; and the bushel he identifies as a Latin measure nearly the same as the English peck, adding that as they were commonly of wood such articles must often have been turned out from a carpenter's shop. On the last verse he finds the English form misleading or at least ambiguous: it is not simply, let your light so shine that men may glorify, but thus, like the lamp on its stand, let your light shine. The motive to publicity he holds the direct opposite of the temper which led the Pharisee to his ostentatious prayers and almsgiving, not to be seen of men and win their praise, but to win men, through our use of a light we know to be not our own, to glorify the Giver of the light; and he finds a partial fulfilment of the command in the impression made on the heathen world by the new life of the church, when they confessed in spite of all prejudices how these Christians loved one another. The name of the Father in heaven he notes was in common use among devout Jews, but its first occurrence in our Lord's teaching deserves to be marked. Barnes explains the figure plainly: salt renders food pleasant and palatable and preserves from putrefaction, and so Christians by their lives and instructions are to keep the world from entire moral corruption, bringing down by their prayers the blessing of God and saving the world by their influence and example from universal vice and crime. On the loss of savour he reasons from chemistry: the salt used in his own country is a chemical compound, and if the saltness were lost there would be nothing remaining, since it enters into the very nature of the substance; but in eastern countries the salt used was impure, mingled with vegetable and earthy substances, so that it might lose the whole of its saltness and a considerable quantity of earthy matter remain, which was good for nothing except, as it is said, to be placed in paths. The light of the world he observes often denotes the sun, which renders objects visible and shows their form and nature and beauties and deformities; the term is often applied to religious teachers and pre-eminently to Jesus, because he is in the moral world what the sun is in the natural, while the apostles and Christian ministers and all Christians are lights because by their instructions and examples they show what God requires and what is the way of duty and peace and happiness. Many of the cities of Judea, he adds, were placed on the summits or sides of mountains and could be seen from afar, as was the case with Jerusalem. The lamp he reads for its purpose: the very reason why they were enlightened was that others might also see the light and be benefited by it, and when men light a candle they do not conceal the light but place it where it may be of use. On the shining he insists the motive is not simply that we should be seen, which would be pride and ostentation, but that being seen God may be honoured: the Pharisees acted to be seen of men, while true Christians act to glorify God and care little what men think of them, except as by their conduct others may be brought to honour God. Robertson takes the verb for losing savour from a root meaning dull or sluggish or foolish, so that it means to play the fool, and of salt to become tasteless and insipid; he reports that it is common in Syria and Palestine to see salt scattered in piles on the ground because it has lost its flavour, the most worthless thing imaginable, and suspects that Jesus may have used a current proverb. The bushel he insists is not a bushel but the bushel, the figure being taken from lowly cottage life: there was a projecting stone in the wall on which the lamp was set, and the house consisted of a single room so that the tiny light sufficed for all; the bushel was an earthenware grain measure, the only one in the room, and the lamp was not put under it save to put it out or to hide it. The stand he insists is a lamp-stand and not a candlestick, as in each of the twelve examples in the Bible, there being the one lamp-stand for the single room; and the adverb even so he says points backward to that lamp-stand, since light shines to see others by and not to call attention to itself.

Calvin applies to the persons what belongs to the doctrine: when Christ calls the apostles the salt of the earth he means that it is their office to season men, because men have nothing in them but what is tasteless until they have been seasoned with the salt of heavenly doctrine. Having reminded them of their calling he pronounces against them a heavy and dreadful judgment if they do not fulfil their duty, for the doctrine entrusted to them is so closely connected with a good conscience and a devout and upright life that corruption which might be tolerated in others would in them be detestable and monstrous: if other men are tasteless in the sight of God, to the apostles is given the salt which imparts a relish to them, but if they have lost their taste, where shall they obtain the remedy they ought to supply to others? He follows the metaphor further, observing that other things when they lose their original qualities are still useful after they have become corrupted, whereas spoiled salt becomes even hurtful and communicates barrenness. The light he applies in two stages: we are all the children of light after having been enlightened by faith, and are commanded to carry burning lamps in our hands that we may not wander in darkness and even to point out to others the way of life; but since the preaching of the Gospel was committed to the apostles above others, and is now committed to the pastors of the church, the designation is given to them in a peculiar manner, and they are placed in that rank on the condition that they shall shine from an elevated situation on all others. The two comparisons mean that they ought to live as if the eyes of all were upon them; and certainly, he adds, the more eminent a person is the more injury he does by a bad example if he acts improperly, so that the apostles must be more careful to live a devout and holy life than unknown persons of the common rank. On the last verse he meets the apparent contradiction with the later command to seek concealment for our good works: that command is intended only to forbid ostentation, while here Christ has quite a different object in view, to recommend to them the glory of God alone. And he draws a consequence: if the glory of good works cannot properly be ascribed to God unless they are traced to him and he is acknowledged to be their only Author, then we cannot without offering an open and gross insult to God extol free will, as if good works proceeded wholly or in part from its power; and he bids us observe how graciously God deals with us when he calls them good. Gill reads the salt of the disciples and apostles of Christ, who might be compared to salt because of the savoury doctrines they preached, as all doctrines are which are agreeable to the Scriptures and of the evangelic kind, full of Christ, serving to exalt him and to magnify the grace of God, suitable to the experiences of the saints and according to godliness; and also because of their savoury lives and conversations, whereby they recommended and gave sanction to the doctrines they preached, being examples to the saints and checks upon wicked men. They were the salt of the earth, that is, of the inhabitants of the earth, not of the land of Judea only where they first lived and preached, but of the whole world into which they were afterwards sent. The light he explains by the luminaries: what the sun and moon are in the heavens with respect to corporal light, the apostles were in the world with regard to spiritual light, carrying and spreading the light of the Gospel not only in Judea but all over the world, which was in great darkness of ignorance and error, and through a divine blessing attending their ministry many were turned from the darkness of Judaism and heathenism and of sin and infidelity to the marvellous light of divine grace; and he notes that the Jews were wont to say of the Israelites in general, and particularly of their council and their learned doctors, what Christ more truly applies here to his apostles. The candle he reads impersonally, a candle is not lighted, and takes it for the Gospel and the gifts qualifying men to preach it, which he then works out at length: it was lighted in the evening of the Jewish dispensation though not confined to the land of Judea, has shone throughout the world, is as a candle to be removed and has been removed from place to place, gives light more or less wherever it is set and dispels darkness, is useful both to work by and to walk with, does not always burn alike clearly and needs looking after, has its thieves as candles sometimes have, and will give the greatest light towards the close of the world, as candles usually do when ready to go out. On the shining he says Christ applies the foregoing simile and opens its design, that the light of the Gospel and the spiritual knowledge of the mysteries of grace which he had communicated to them were to be openly declared and made manifest before men, light being given not merely for their own private use but for the public good of mankind, so that being placed as lights in the world they were to hold forth the word of light and life in the most open and conspicuous manner.

Clarke states the office briefly, that our Lord shows here what the preachers of the Gospel and all who profess to follow him should be, the salt of the earth to preserve the world from putrefaction and destruction. On the possibility of salt losing its savour he settles the question by testimony, quoting the traveller Maundrell on the Valley of Salt: along one side of the valley there is a small precipice occasioned by the continual taking away of the salt, in which the veins of it may be seen, and a piece broken from it had in the part exposed to the rain and sun and air perfectly lost its savour though it still had the sparks and particles of salt, while the inner part which was connected to the rock retained its savour. The light of the world he explains as the instruments which God chooses to make use of to illuminate the minds of men, as he uses the sun, to which Clarke thinks our Lord probably pointed, to enlighten the world; and he reports that light of the world was a title applied to the most eminent rabbis, which Christ transfers from them and gives to his own disciples, who by the doctrines he taught them were to be the means of diffusing the light of life throughout the universe. For the city he again quotes his traveller, on the small rising to the north of Tabor which they call the Mount of Beatitudes, and the city Saphet not far from that little hill. The bushel he identifies as a measure among both Greeks and Romans containing a little more than an English peck, and adds from ancient writers that only those who had bad designs hid a candle under a bushel, that in the dead of the night when all were asleep they might rise up and have light at hand to help them effect their horrid purposes. On the shining he renders the Greek more literally as thus let your light shine, and expounds it by the two figures: as the sun is lighted up in the firmament to diffuse its light and heat freely to every inhabitant of the earth, and as the lamp is not set under the bushel but placed upon the lamp-stand that it may give light to all in the house, thus let every follower of Christ, and especially every preacher of the Gospel, diffuse the light of heavenly knowledge and the warmth of divine love through the whole circle of their acquaintance. It is not sufficient, he adds, to have light; we must walk in the light and by the light, our whole conduct being a perpetual comment on the doctrine we have received and a constant exemplification of its power and truth.

Henry sets the two figures against the discouragements of the disciples. Christ had lately called them and told them they should be fishers of men, and here he tells them further what he designed them to be, which would encourage and support them under their sufferings, since though they should be treated with contempt they should really be blessings to the world, and the more so for their suffering thus. It was a discouragement to them that they were so few and so weak, and he asks what they could do in so large a province as the whole earth; nothing, if they were to work by force of arms and dint of sword, but being to work silently as salt, one handful of that salt would diffuse its savour far and wide and work insensibly and irresistibly as leaven. The prophets who went before them were the salt of the land of Canaan, but the apostles were the salt of the whole earth, for they must go into all the world to preach the gospel. The doctrine of the gospel he calls salt because it is penetrating and quick and powerful and reaches the heart, because it is cleansing and relishing and preserves from putrefaction; and he recalls that salt was required in all the sacrifices and that an everlasting covenant is called a covenant of salt, as the gospel is an everlasting gospel. Good salt he describes as white and small and broken into many grains but very useful and necessary, quoting Pliny that without salt human life cannot be sustained, and he draws four lessons from it: what they are to be in themselves, seasoned with the salt of grace in thoughts and affections and words and actions, since we must have salt in ourselves or we cannot diffuse it among others; what they are to be to others, not only good but doing good, insinuating themselves into the minds of the people not to serve any secular interest of their own but to transform them into the taste and relish of the gospel; what great blessings they are to the world, mankind lying in ignorance and wickedness having been a vast heap of unsavoury stuff ready to putrefy until Christ sent forth his disciples by their lives and doctrines to season it with knowledge and grace; and how they must expect to be disposed of, not laid on a heap nor continuing always together at Jerusalem, but scattered as salt upon the meat, here a grain and there a grain, as the Levites were dispersed in Israel, that wherever they live they may communicate their savour. Of the salt that has lost its savour he says the case is very sad, and makes it threefold: he is irrecoverable, since salt is a remedy for unsavoury meat but there is no remedy for unsavoury salt, and if Christianity does not give a man a relish nothing will; he is unprofitable, good thenceforth for nothing, as a man without reason, so a Christian without grace, and a wicked Christian the worst of men; and he is doomed to rejection, expelled the church and the communion of the faithful to which he is a blot and a burden. The light he says bespeaks them useful as the former figure did but more glorious, and he quotes the saying that nothing is more useful than the sun and salt; all Christians are light in the Lord and must shine as lights, but ministers in a special manner, Christ calling himself the Light of the world while they are workers together with him and have some of his honour put upon them, borrowing and deriving their light from him. The similitude he explains in two things. As lights of the world they are illustrious and conspicuous with many eyes upon them, like a city set on a hill which cannot be hid; the disciples of Christ, especially those forward and zealous in his service, become remarkable and are taken notice of as beacons, so that all their neighbours have an eye upon them, some admiring and commending and studying to imitate them, others envying and hating and censuring and studying to blast them, and they are therefore concerned to walk circumspectly because of their observers, being as spectacles to the world. And as lights they are intended to illuminate and give light to others, so that they shall be set up as lights and must shine as lights, by their good preaching, communicating the knowledge they have for the good of others and not burying the talent in a napkin, and by their good living, being burning and shining lights that evidence in their whole conversation that they are indeed followers of Christ. On the manner of the shining he is exact: our light must shine by doing such good works as men may see and approve of, works of good report among them that are without; we must do good works that may be seen to the edification of others, but not that they may be seen to our own ostentation, for we are bid to pray in secret, and what lies between God and our souls must be kept to ourselves, while that which is of itself open and obvious to the sight of men we must study to make congruous to our profession. The gospel itself he adds is so strong a light, and carries with it so much of its own evidence, that like a city on a hill it cannot be hid but must appear to be from God to all who do not wilfully shut their eyes against it; and those to whom it does not give light must thank themselves, since they will not be in the house with it nor make a diligent and impartial enquiry into it.

debates: Whether salt can in fact lose its savour, where Barnes reasons from the chemistry that the salt of his own country could not, saltness entering into the very nature of the substance, but that eastern salt was impure and might lose the whole of its saltness and leave the earthy matter behind, Clarke settles the question affirmatively from Maundrell's report of the Valley of Salt, Ellicott reports the same traveller and the rock-salt of the Dead Sea shore but adds that he knows of no recent confirmation, and Robertson answers from common observation that salt lying in piles on the ground because it has lost its flavour is a familiar sight in Syria and Palestine, and suspects a current proverb behind the saying.

Who is addressed in the two figures, where Calvin restricts the designation in a peculiar manner to the apostles and now to the pastors of the church, Gill reads it of the disciples and apostles, Barnes extends it to the apostles, to Christian ministers and to all Christians, Henry grants it to Christians generally but to ministers in a special manner, and Ellicott takes the disciples in their ideal character as the germ of a new Israel called to a prophetic work.

How the command to let the light be seen stands with the later command to hide our good works, where Calvin answers that the later precept forbids ostentation only while here the object is the glory of God alone, Barnes that it is not right to do a thing merely to be seen, which is pride, but that being seen God may be honoured, Ellicott that the motive is the direct opposite of the Pharisee's ostentation, and Henry that we must do good works that may be seen to the edification of others but not to our own ostentation.
outliers: Gill works the candle out as a figure of the Gospel at length, lighted in the evening of the Jewish dispensation, needing to be looked after, having its thieves as candles sometimes have, and giving its greatest light towards the close of the world.
Clarke reports from ancient writers that only those with bad designs hid a candle under a bushel, that in the dead of night they might rise with a light ready for their purposes.

Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.

17.pericope_label: Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil. For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled. Whosoever therefore shall break one of these least commandments, and shall teach men so, he shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven: but whosoever shall do and teach them, the same shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven. For I say unto you, That except your righteousness shall exceed the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, ye shall in no case enter into the kingdom of heaven.

schools.summary: Ellicott marks a new section beginning here and running to the end of the chapter: from the ideal picture of the life of the society he came to found, our Lord passes to a protest against the current teaching of the scribes, who sometimes adhered to the letter and neglected the spirit and sometimes overrode even the letter by unauthorised traditions, lowering the standard of righteousness to the level of men's practices instead of raising their practices to the standard God had fixed. The words think not he says imply that men had begun so to think, the Teacher who came preaching repentance but also promising forgiveness being supposed to attack the authority of the two great channels through which the will of God had been revealed; the law and the prophets were popularly equivalent to the whole of the Old Testament, though a strict classification required the addition of the holy writings. On the word of solemn affirmation he dwells at its first occurrence: it is the familiar Amen of the church's worship, used in the same way in the worship of the wilderness and of the Temple, coming from the Hebrew root for fixed and steadfast and true, used for solemn affirmation or solemn prayer, and passing from the synagogue into the Christian church, where by the time the Gospels were written it had become so familiar that all the Evangelists used it without hesitation, sometimes singly and in John uniformly with the emphasis of reduplication. The formula about heaven and earth passing he takes to have been one in common use with our Lord to express the unchangeableness of the divine word. On the least commandments he argues against the ceremonial sense: the words seem at first to imply that even the ceremonial law was to be binding in its full extent upon Christ's disciples, but the usage of the time confined the word to the moral laws of God, throughout the New Testament it is never used in any other sense with one possible exception, and the context, which proceeds at once to deal with moral laws and does not touch on ceremonial, agrees with that meaning; the least commandments are therefore those which seemed trivial yet were really great, the control of thoughts and desires and words as compared with the apparently greater commands that dealt with acts. The reference to teaching he takes to show that our Lord was speaking to his disciples as the future instructors of mankind, and that the obvious import of his words is that they were to raise and not lower the standard of righteousness previously recognised. On the scribes he notes their first mention in our Lord's teaching, and that the frequent combination of the two words implies that for the most part they were of the school of the Pharisees, as the chief priests were for the most part of that of the Sadducees; and he traces the word, which in the Old Testament means simply the man who writes, the secretary or registrar of the king's edicts, and after the return from Babylon was used first of the transcribers and editors of the sacred books and then by a natural transition of their interpreters, which is its dominant sense in the New Testament, these being much occupied with the traditional comments of previous teachers. Barnes places the saying at the opening of the work, when it was important to state what he came to do, since by setting up to be a teacher in opposition to the scribes and Pharisees some might charge him with an intention to destroy their law and abolish the customs of the nation; to destroy he glosses as to abrogate, to deny their divine authority, to set men free from the obligation to obey them, and to fulfil as to complete the design, to fill up what was predicted, to accomplish what was intended. The jot he identifies as the name of the smallest letter in the Hebrew alphabet and the tittle as the small points or apices which serve to distinguish one letter from another, so that to change a small point of one letter might vary the meaning of a word and destroy the sense; hence the Jews were exceedingly cautious in writing those letters and considered the smallest change or omission a reason for destroying the whole manuscript when they were transcribing the Old Testament, and the expression one jot or tittle became proverbial. On the least commandments he says the Pharisees probably divided the precepts of the law into lesser and greater, teaching that those who violated the former were guilty of a trivial offence only, and that Christ teaches that in his kingdom they who make this distinction, or who taught that any laws of God might be violated with impunity, should be in no esteem and not be regarded as proper religious teachers, while those should be held in high regard who observed all the laws of God without distinction. The righteousness of the scribes he describes as external and not real holiness, consisting in outward observances of the ceremonial and traditional law: they offered sacrifices, fasted often, prayed much, were very punctilious about ablutions and tithes and the ceremonies of religion, but neglected justice and truth and purity and holiness of heart and did not strive to be pure in their motives before God, whereas the righteousness Jesus required in his kingdom was purity, chastity, honesty, temperance, the fear of God and the love of man. Lightfoot supplies the Jewish background in three steps. It was the opinion of the nation concerning the Messiah that he would bring in a new law, but not at all to the prejudice of Moses and the prophets, and that he would advance the Mosaic law to the very highest pitch and fulfil what the prophets foretold according to the letter and even to the greatest pomp. The scribes and Pharisees therefore snatched an occasion of cavilling against Christ and readily objected that he was not the true Messiah because he abolished the doctrines of the traditions which they obtruded upon the people for Moses and the prophets. He meets this prejudice by several arguments: that he abolished not the law when he abolished traditions, since he came that he might fulfil the law; that not one iota shall perish from the law; and that he brought in an observation of the law much more pure and excellent than the Pharisaical observation of it was. On the asseveration he notes that such a form was usual to the nation though with the syllables somewhat changed, and quotes the gloss that in truth is a manner of speech used in swearing; but our Saviour uses the phrase by the highest divine right, because he is the Amen, the faithful witness, and because he published the gospel, the highest truth. By this asseveration, Lightfoot adds, he well opposes his divine oracles against the insolent madness of the traditional doctors, who did often vent their blasphemous and frivolous tales under this very seal, saying that they speak in truth, and holding that wheresoever this is said it is a tradition of Moses from Sinai.

Calvin explains why the declaration was needed. Christ might justly have maintained the perfection of his life, but here he treats of doctrine and not of life. Since he had raised the minds of men with unusual expectation and even admitted disciples by baptism, it is probable that many were in a state of suspense and doubt and were eagerly inquiring what was the design of that novelty; and he now declares that his doctrine is so far from being at variance with the law that it agrees perfectly with it and brings its complete fulfilment. Two reasons he finds for the declaration. As soon as any new method of teaching makes its appearance, the body of the people immediately look upon it as if everything were to be overturned, and the preaching of the Gospel had raised the expectation that the church would assume a totally different form from what had previously belonged to it, the ancient and accustomed government being thought about to be abolished; and this opinion was in many respects very dangerous, for devout worshippers of God would never have embraced the Gospel if it had been a revolt from the law, while light and turbulent spirits would eagerly have seized on an occasion for entirely overthrowing the state of religion, since we know in what insolent freaks rash people indulge when there is anything new. Besides, Christ saw that the greater part of the Jews, though they professed to believe the Law, were profane and degenerate, and the condition of the people was so decayed and everything filled with so many corruptions. On the permanence of the law he dismisses an ingenious refinement: some indulge in refinements on the particle, as if the day of judgment were to put an end to the law, and he grants that since tongues shall then cease and prophecies be abolished he thinks the written law as well as the exposition of it will come to an end; but being of opinion that Christ spoke more simply, he does not choose to feed the ears of readers with such amusements, and asks only that we hold that sooner shall heaven fall to pieces and the whole frame of the world become a mass of confusion than the stability of the law give way.
