The fulfilling down to the smallest point he refers not to the life of men, since even those regenerated by the Spirit of God are very far from keeping the law perfectly, but to the perfect truth of the doctrine: there is nothing in the law that is unimportant and nothing that was put there at random, and so it is impossible that a single letter shall perish. The commandments he says are expressly the commandments of life, the ten words which all the children of God ought to take as the rule of their life, so that those are false and deceitful teachers who do not restrain their disciples within obedience to the law and are unworthy to occupy a place in the church if they weaken its authority in the slightest degree, while those are honest and faithful ministers of God who recommend the keeping of the law both by word and by example. The epithet least he calls an expression used in accommodation to the judgment of men, since though the commandments have not all the same weight we are not at liberty to think anything little on which the heavenly Legislator has been pleased to issue a command; for what sacrilege is it to treat contemptuously anything which has proceeded from his sacred mouth, which is to sink his majesty to the rank of creatures. On the last verse he takes a passing notice of those who laboured to throw a stain on the doctrine of the Gospel as if it were the ruin of the Law, pointing out briefly that nothing has less influence over their minds than zeal for the law: they pretend that their hostility arises from a strong desire that the law should not be violated, but their life makes it evident how coldly they observe it, and how unconcerned they are about mocking God while they boast before men of an assumed and hypocritical righteousness. But he raises a further question which he thinks deserves inquiry, and here parts from most interpreters: whether Christ does not rather blame the corrupted manner of teaching which the scribes followed in instructing the people, since by confining the law of God to outward duties only they trained their disciples, like apes, to hypocrisy. He admits that they lived as ill as they taught and even worse, and therefore willingly includes their hypocritical parade of false righteousness along with their corrupted doctrine; but the principal charge brought by Christ against their doctrine may be easily learned from what follows in the discourse, where he removes from the law their false and wicked interpretations and restores it to its purity, so that the objection unjustly brought against him by the scribes is powerfully thrown back on themselves.

Clarke takes the verb for destroying through its parts, from a preposition and a word meaning to loose or violate or dissolve: do not imagine that I am come to violate the law, to make it of none effect, to dissolve the connection which subsists between its several parts or the obligation men are under to have their lives regulated by its moral precepts, nor to dissolve the connecting reference it has to the good things promised; but I am come to complete, to perfect its connection and reference, to accomplish everything shadowed forth in the Mosaic ritual, to fill up its great design, and to give grace to all my followers to fill up every moral duty. Christ completed the law, he says, in two ways: in itself, since it was only the shadow and typical representation of good things to come, and he added to it that which was necessary to make it perfect, his own sacrifice, without which it could neither satisfy God nor sanctify men; and in himself, by submitting to its types with an exact obedience and verifying them. On the permanence he hears in the opening of the ministry a teaching about the instability of all visible things: the heaven which you see, and which is so glorious, and the earth which you inhabit and love, shall pass away, for the things which are seen are temporal while the things which are not seen are ever-during, and the word of the Lord endures for ever. The jot he identifies as the smallest letter in the Hebrew alphabet and the tittle as either those points which serve for vowels in that language, if they then existed, or the seraphs or points of certain letters, the change of any of which into another would make a most essential alteration in the sense, or as the rabbins say destroy the world; or, he suggests, our Lord may refer to the little ornaments which certain letters assume on their tops, which cause them to appear like small branches, and he lists the letters which can take such coronal apices. On the least commandments he notes that the Pharisees were remarkable for making a distinction between weightier and lighter matters in the law, and between what has been called in a corrupt part of the Christian church mortal and venial sins; and he calls it an awful consideration that he who by his mode of acting or speaking or explaining the words of God sets the holy precept aside, or explains away its force and meaning, shall have no place in the kingdom of Christ here nor in the kingdom of glory above. The exceeding righteousness he glosses as abounding more, unless it take in not only the letter but the spirit and design of the moral and ritual precept, the one directing how to walk so as to please God and the other pointing out Christ the great Atonement through whom a sinner is enabled to do so; and he adds that the old English word for righteousness is right-wiseness, that is, complete and thorough and excellent wisdom. Wesley puts the first clause as a triple caution, do not imagine, fear, hope, that I am come like your teachers to destroy the law or the prophets; and the fulfilling as to establish, illustrate and explain the law's highest meaning, both by his life and by his doctrine. The phrase till all things shall be effected he expounds as what the law either requires or foretells, and he gives the law a double effect: it has its effect when the rewards are given and the punishments annexed to it inflicted, as well as when its precepts are obeyed. The least commandment he says is so accounted by men, and the teaching may be either by word or by example, while to be the least in the kingdom of heaven means to have no part therein.

Henry frames the whole passage by the two things to which his hearers looked in their religion, the scriptures of the Old Testament as their rule, wherein Christ shows them they were in the right, and the scribes and Pharisees as their example, wherein he shows them they were in the wrong. The rule Christ came to establish, he says, exactly agreed with the scriptures of the Old Testament, here called the law and the prophets, the prophets being commentators upon the law and both together making up that rule of faith and practice which Christ found upon the throne in the Jewish church and here keeps on the throne. He then distinguishes the parties addressed: let not the pious Jews, who have an affection for the law and the prophets, fear that he comes to destroy them, nor be prejudiced against Christ and his doctrine from a jealousy that this kingdom would derogate from the honour of the scriptures which they had embraced as coming from God and of which they had experienced the power and purity; and let not the profane Jews, who are disaffected to the law and weary of that yoke, hope that he is come to destroy it, nor let carnal libertines imagine that the Messiah is come to discharge them from the obligation of divine precepts and yet to secure to them divine promises. Christ commands nothing now which was forbidden either by the law of nature or the moral law, nor forbids anything which those laws had enjoined, and he takes care here to rectify the mistake. The fulfilling Henry gives in five senses: to obey the commands of the law, since he was made under the law and in all respects yielded obedience to it, honouring his parents, sanctifying the sabbath, praying, giving alms, and obeying perfectly as none other ever did; to make good the promises of the law and the predictions of the prophets, which all bore witness to him, the covenant of grace being for substance the same then as now and Christ the Mediator of it; to answer the types of the law, so that, as Tillotson expresses it, he did not make void but make good the ceremonial law and manifested himself to be the Substance of all those shadows; to fill up its defects and so to complete and perfect it, which is what the word properly signifies, so that if we consider the law as a vessel that had some water in it before, he did not come to pour out the water but to fill the vessel up to the brim, or as a picture first rough-drawn which displays some outlines only and is afterwards filled up; and to carry on the same design, the Christian institutes being so far from thwarting the main design of the Jewish religion that they promote it to the highest degree, the gospel being not the repeal of the law but the amendment of it and consequently its establishment. The perpetuity he presses by the speaker's own authority, that he who declares it is the Amen, the faithful Witness, and he observes that the care of God concerning his law extends itself even to those things that seem of least account in it, the iotas and the tittles, since whatever belongs to God and bears his stamp, be it ever so little, shall be preserved; the laws of men are conscious to themselves of so much imperfection that they allow it for a maxim that the extreme points of the law are not the law, but God will stand by and maintain every iota and every tittle of his. Among the commands of God he grants there are some less than others, none absolutely little but comparatively so, and notes that the Jews reckoned the least of the commandments to be that of the bird's nest, which yet had an intention very great and considerable. To disannul the least of God's commands, in doctrine or in practice, he calls a dangerous thing, since to break them is to go about either to contract their extent or weaken their obligation, which is something more than transgressing the law, it is making void the law; and the further such corruptions spread the worse they are, for it is impudence enough to break the command but a greater degree of it to teach men so, which refers to those who then sat in Moses' seat and by their comments corrupted and perverted the text. Of the scribes and Pharisees he owns what was commendable: they were much in fasting and prayer and giving of alms, punctual in observing the ceremonial appointments, and made it their business to teach others, and had such an interest with the people that they were looked upon as super-conformable to the law, so that it was a great surprise to hear that men must be better than they or not go to heaven. But he distinguishes the two righteousnesses point by point: they were partial in the law and laid most stress upon the ritual part of it, while we must be universal and not think it enough to give the priest his tithe but must give God our hearts; they minded only the outside, while we must make conscience of inside godliness; they aimed at the praise and applause of men, while we must aim at acceptance with God; and they were proud of what they did in religion and trusted to it as a righteousness, while we, when we have done all, must deny ourselves and say that we are unprofitable servants and trust only to the righteousness of Christ.

debates: What it means to fulfil the law, where Henry distinguishes five senses, to obey its commands, to make good its promises, to answer its types, to fill up its defects as a vessel is filled to the brim or a rough-drawn picture completed, and to carry on the same design, Clarke reads the word as complete and makes the completion consist in Christ's own sacrifice added to what was only a shadow, Wesley has him establish, illustrate and explain its highest meaning by life and doctrine, and Barnes keeps to filling up what was predicted and accomplishing what was intended.

What till all be fulfilled refers to, where Calvin refuses the refinement that the day of judgment will end the law, declining to feed his readers' ears with such amusements, and insists that the words refer not to the life of men, since even the regenerate keep the law imperfectly, but to the perfect truth of a doctrine in which nothing was put at random, while Wesley gives the law a double effect and holds that it is fulfilled when the rewards are given and the punishments inflicted as well as when its precepts are obeyed, and Barnes reads it simply as until its whole design shall be accomplished.

What is charged against the scribes and Pharisees in the closing verse, where Calvin notes that most commentators take it of their lives but asks whether the corrupted manner of teaching is not rather in view, since by confining the law to outward duties they trained their disciples like apes to hypocrisy, and willingly includes both, while Barnes makes the charge simply that their righteousness was external and not real holiness, and Henry first grants them what was commendable and then distinguishes the two righteousnesses point by point.
outliers: Henry observes that human laws confess their own imperfection by the maxim that the extreme points of the law are not the law, whereas God will maintain every iota and tittle of his.
Lightfoot shows the traditional doctors using the very seal of this asseveration, saying that they speak in truth, and holding that wherever this is said it is a tradition of Moses from Sinai.
themes: Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.
For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled.

Whosoever therefore shall break one of these least commandments, and shall teach men so, he shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven: but whosoever shall do and teach them, the same shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.
For I say unto you, That except your righteousness shall exceed the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, ye shall in no case enter into the kingdom of heaven.

21.pericope_label: Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not kill; and whosoever shall kill shall be in danger of the judgment: But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire. Therefore if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee; Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift. Agree with thine adversary quickly, whiles thou art in the way with him; lest at any time the adversary deliver thee to the judge, and the judge deliver thee to the officer, and thou be cast into prison. Verily I say unto thee, Thou shalt by no means come out thence, till thou hast paid the uttermost farthing.

schools.summary: Ellicott settles the construction first: there is no reasonable doubt that the marginal reading, to them of old time, is right, the construction being identical with several in the Epistles and the Revelation. Two questions then present themselves, who they of old time were and who spoke the words quoted. The words are very general and, as interpreted by the use of the phrase elsewhere, seem to point to the time when synagogues began to be established, that is, after the return from Babylon. As to the speaker, the impersonal form, the contrast between it was said and I say unto you, and the tone of authority imposing a new law for that which it supersedes seem to him conclusive against referring the words, even when they are found in the Law, to that Law as given by God through Moses; the stress lies on the words, ye heard that it was said, which is to say, this was the report of the Law given you by your teachers in school and synagogue, while I give you another and truer report. The emphatic I of the next verse he marks as probably the chief cause of the wonder expressed at the end of the Sermon, since the scribe in his teaching invariably referred to this Rabbi and that while the new Teacher spoke as one having a higher authority of his own. The three words without a cause he reports wanting in many of the best manuscripts: they may have been inserted to soften down the apparent harshness of the teaching, though if so it must have been at an early date, before the fourth century; or they may have been in the text originally and struck out as giving too wide a margin to vain and vague excuses. Ethically he is careful that the teaching is not that the emotion of anger, with or without a cause, stands on the same level of guilt with murder, but that the former so soon expands and explodes into the latter that it will be brought to trial and sentenced according to the merits of each case, the occasion of the anger and the degree in which it has been checked or cherished. The altar he paints as a scene in the Jewish Temple: the worshipper is about to offer a gift, the most generic term being intentionally used to represent any kind of offering, and stands at the altar with the priest waiting to do his work, and that is the right time for recollection and self-scrutiny, the question for him being not whether he has a ground of complaint against any one but whether any one has cause of complaint against him. To leave the gift and the priest with the act of sacrifice unfinished he grants would appear to men a breach of liturgical propriety and would be strange and startling, yet that were better than to sacrifice with the sense of a wrong unconfessed and unatoned for, and still better than the deeper evil of not being ready to forgive; and he cites the curious Talmudic rule to which the words may allude, that if a man is on the point of offering the Passover and remembers that there is leaven left in the house, he should return and remove it and then come and finish the Passover, so that what the scribes laid down as a duty in regard to the leaven of bread our Lord applies to the leaven of malice and wickedness. Being reconciled, he insists, is not enough understood as a command to remove ill-will from our own mind, though that is implied; there must also be confession of wrong and the endeavour to make amends. With the adversary the imagery changes and returns to that of human tribunals: the man whom we have wronged appears as the prosecutor bringing his charge against us, and the impulse of the natural man at such a time, even if conscious of wrong, is to make the best of his case, to prevaricate, to recriminate, whereas the truer wisdom is to be on good terms with him, showing our own good will and so winning his. The whole teaching, he observes, is obviously addressed to one who has done wrong, the treatment of a false charge involving different considerations. In the application he divides the figure: the judge is clearly God, the officers are those, angels or others, who execute his judgment, and the adversary is those whom we have wronged, leaving the wrong unredressed; the devil is described elsewhere as the great adversary, and that meaning is perhaps not excluded though it is not prominent here, since any evil deed becomes in the end as an accusing Satan bearing its witness against us. The farthing he identifies from the Latin as the fourth part of a small coin, the mite being half of it and the smallest coin in circulation, and notes that the farthing of a later chapter is a different word. Whether the words point to a terminable or an endless punishment he asks without deciding: within the framework of the similitude such a sentence would not involve perpetual imprisonment if only the condemned could get together the money to pay his debt or fine, and we might infer, as Romanist divines have inferred, that such a payment followed by liberation was possible in the divine judgment; but in practice, unless the man had friends or property, the sentence would for the most part involve a life-long punishment, and he asks whether, when we turn to the realities shadowed forth in the parable, a man can pay the uttermost farthing in that unseen world. Barnes says Jesus proceeds here to comment on prevailing opinions among the Jews in order to show that the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees was defective and that men needed a better righteousness; by them of old time he would rather render to the ancients, and thinks the reference is to the interpreters of the law and the prophets rather than to Moses, since Jesus did not set himself against the law of Moses but against the false and pernicious interpretations of it prevalent in his time. The commandment he says literally denotes taking the life of another with malice, and the Jews understood it as meaning no more, while the comment of our Saviour shows that it was spiritual and designed to extend to the thoughts and feelings as well as the external act. The right to expound it he grounds in the speaker: Jesus being God as well as man, and therefore being the original Giver of the law, had a right to expound it or change it as he pleased, and he therefore spoke here as having authority and not as the scribes; it may be added, Barnes says, that no mere man ever spake as Jesus did when explaining or enforcing the law, and that he who has a right to ordain and change laws in the government of God must himself be divine. Anger he defines as that feeling which we have when we are injured and which prompts us to defend ourselves when in danger, a natural feeling given to us as a natural expression of our disapprobation of evil conduct and that we may defend ourselves when suddenly attacked; when excited against sin it is lawful, since God is angry with the wicked and Jesus looked on the hypocritical Pharisees with anger, and we are told to be angry and sin not; what our Saviour speaks of here is anger without a cause, unjustly, rashly, hastily. The altar he reads against the Pharisees, who were intent only on the external act in worship and looked not at all to the internal acts of the mind, thinking a man did well if he conformed to the external rites however much envy and malice and secret hatred he had; our Saviour taught a different doctrine, that it was of more consequence to have the heart right than to perform the outward act, and that a man who had gone so far as to bring his gift to the very altar should leave his offering there and go and be reconciled, not waiting till the offended brother should come to him but going and seeking him out. On the adversary he continues the illustration of the sixth commandment: to be in hostility, to go to law, to be litigious, is always a violation on one side or the other of the law requiring us to love our neighbour, and while you are going to the court, before the trial has taken place, it is your duty if possible to come to an agreement, it being wrong to carry the contention to a court of law. The consequence of not being reconciled he says is expressed in the language of courts, the adversary delivering you to the judge and he to the executioner and he throwing you into prison; Jesus did not mean to say that this would literally be the way with God, but that God's dealings with those who harbour these feelings were represented by the punishment inflicted by human tribunals, holding all such as violators of the sixth commandment. And Barnes adds a caution of his own: there is no propriety in the use sometimes made of this verse, in regarding God as the adversary of the sinner and urging him on that ground to be reconciled. Lightfoot reads the formula as tradition: ye have heard means ye have received it by tradition, and the phrase about them of old time means that it is an old tradition, for the passages of the law cited here by our Saviour are not produced as the bare words of Moses but as clothed in the glosses of the scribes, which appears most plainly in the clause about killing being guilty of the judgment, holding out as it does the false paint of tradition and misrepresenting the law so as to make it of none effect; and if it be asked why Christ makes mention of those of old time, Lightfoot answers that the memory of the ancienter fathers of the traditions was venerable among the people. The words but I say he calls the words of one that refutes or determines a question, very frequently met with in the Hebrew writers, and he brings in the Jewish commentators to show that the teacher of the prophecy was understood to be the Messiah. On the word brother he gives the schools' distinction, that a brother signifies an Israelite by nation and blood while a neighbour signifies an Israelite in religion and worship, that is, a proselyte. On the altar he quotes the rules the Jews restrained to pecuniary damages, that he who offers an oblation without restoring what he had unjustly taken away does not do his duty, and that he who steals anything from his neighbour, though it be but a farthing, and swears falsely, is bound to restitution, meeting the wronged party half way, and that he who swears falsely about the smallest coin is bound to inquire after the owner even as far as the islands in the sea and to make restitution; and he observes how provision is there made for pecuniary damages only and bare restitution, which might be done without a charitable mind and a brotherly heart, where Christ urges more. To leave the gift before the altar he says was altogether unusual in such a cause, though the Hebrew lawyers speak much of sacrifices delayed or even rejected when a blemish was discovered at the altar or some uncleanness appeared in the offerer. The way with the adversary he glosses from the parallel as going with him to the magistrate, where there is a clear distinction between the magistrate and the judge, so that the sense is, does your neighbour accuse you of some damage or of money due to him, and are you now going to the bench of three to commence the suit? Compound with your adversary, lest he compel you to some higher tribunal where your danger will be greater. The farthing he works out from both Talmuds, giving the whole table of small coins down to the smallest piece, of which Maimonides says that what is not worth it is not to be reckoned among riches.

Calvin connects this sentence with what has gone before, our Lord explaining more fully, by minute instances, by what tortuous methods the Pharisees debased the law so that their righteousness is mere filth. But it is a mistake, he insists, to suppose that this is a correction or enlargement of the Law, or that Christ raises his disciples to a higher degree of perfection than he could raise a gross and carnal nation scarcely able to learn first principles. It has been a prevailing opinion that the beginning of righteousness was laid down in the ancient law but that the perfection of it is pointed out in the Gospel; and nothing, he says, was farther from the design of Christ than to alter or innovate anything in the commandments of the law, since there God has once fixed the rule of life which he will never retract. But as the law had been corrupted by false expositions and turned to a profane meaning, Christ vindicates it against such corruptions and points out its true meaning, from which the Jews had departed. The reply, he notes, is not opposed to the command of Moses but to the interpretation usually put upon it by the scribes; and since the Pharisees boasted of antiquity, it being always the custom to plead the prescription of a long period in defence of errors, Christ reminds the people of his authority, to which all antiquity ought justly to give way, whence we conclude that truth is of greater weight than custom or the number of years. Three degrees of condemnation he finds assigned besides the violence of the hands, which implies that this precept of the law restrains not only the hands but all affections opposed to brotherly love: those who shall only be angry with their brethren, or treat them with haughty disdain, or injure them by any reproach, are murderers. The middle term he has no doubt is an interjection of contempt or disdain, occupying a place between anger and openly reproachful language; and though Christ adjudges the severest sentence only to those who break out into open reproach, we must not suppose that he declares the others free from a similar punishment. The clause about the altar he says confirms and at the same time explains the preceding doctrine, and amounts to this, that the precept of the law which forbids murder is obeyed when we maintain agreement and brotherly kindness with our neighbour; and to impress this more strongly Christ declares that even the duties of religion are displeasing to God and rejected by him if we are at variance with each other, his meaning being that so long as a difference with our neighbour is kept up by our fault we have no access to God. If the worship men render to God is polluted and corrupted by their resentments, Calvin reasons, this enables us to conclude in what estimation he holds mutual agreement among ourselves. A question may here be put, whether it is not absurd that the duties of charity should be esteemed more highly than the worship of God, since we should then be forced to say either that the order of the law is improper or that the first table must be preferred to the second; and the answer he calls easy, for the words of Christ mean nothing more than this, that it is a false and empty profession of worshipping God which is made by those who act unjustly towards their brethren. On the adversary he parts from the obvious reading: Christ appears to go farther and to exhort to reconciliation not only those who have injured their brethren but those also who are unjustly treated; but Calvin interprets the words as having been spoken with another view, to take away occasion for hatred and resentment and to point out the method of cherishing good-will. For whence come all injuries, he asks, but from this, that each person is too tenacious of his own rights, that is, too much disposed to consult his own convenience to the disadvantage of others, almost all being so blinded by a wicked love of themselves that even in the worst causes they flatter themselves that they are in the right? To meet all hatred and enmity and debate and act of injustice, Christ reproves that obstinacy which is the source of these evils, and enjoins his own people to cultivate moderation and justice and to make some abatement from the highest rigour, that by such an act of justice they may purchase for themselves peace and friendship.

Clarke renders the opening phrase as to or by the ancients, and allows that by the ancients we may understand those who lived before the law as well as those who lived under it, since murder was in the most solemn manner forbidden before as well as under the law; but he thinks it very likely that our Lord refers here merely to traditions and glosses relative to the ancient Mosaic ordinance, such as by their operation rendered the primitive command of little or no effect. Murder from the beginning, he says, has been punished with death, and is probably the only crime that should be punished with death; and he adds his own opinion, that there is much reason to doubt whether the punishment of death inflicted for any other crime is not in itself murder, whatever the authority may be that has instituted it, citing the agreement of the greatest legislators and the arguments lately produced for the amendment of the criminal laws. On the words without a cause he is decided: the Greek means who is vainly incensed, that translation being literal, and the very objectionable phrase without a cause is left out; what our Lord seems to prohibit is not merely that miserable facility which some have of being angry at every trifle, continually taking offence against their best friends, but that anger which leads a man to commit outrages against another and so subject himself to the punishment inflicted on those who break the peace. The word for vainly, he reports, is wanting in the famous Vatican manuscript and two others, in the Ethiopic and the latter Arabic and the Saxon and the Vulgate, in two copies of the old Itala, in Justin Martyr and Ptolomeus and Origen and Tertullian, and in all the ancient copies quoted by Jerome; it was probably a marginal gloss originally, which in process of time crept into the text. The judgment he identifies as the senate of twenty-three magistrates whose business it was to judge in cases of murder and other capital crimes, punishing criminals by strangling or beheading. On the altar he sets the principle that evil must be nipped in the bud, since an unkind thought of another may be the foundation of what leads to actual murder; a Christian, properly speaking, cannot be an enemy to any man, nor is he to consider any man his enemy without the fullest evidence, since surmises to the prejudice of another can never rest in the bosom of him who has the love of God in his heart, to whom all men are brethren, seen as children of God and members of Christ or at least capable of becoming such. If a tender forgiving spirit was required even in a Jew when he approached God's altar with a bullock or a lamb, how much more necessary is this in a man who professes to be a follower of the Lamb of God, especially when he receives the symbols of that Sacrifice which was offered for the life of the world. To leave the gift he reads as a direction not to attempt to bring any offering to God while in a spirit of enmity, or while having a difference with a neighbour which has not been diligently addressed: God will not accept any act of religious worship from us while any enmity subsists in our hearts towards any soul of man, or while any subsists in our neighbour's heart towards us which we have not used the proper means to remove, since a religion the very essence of which is love cannot suffer at its altars a heart that is revengeful and uncharitable. The adversary he identifies as properly a plaintiff in law, a perfect law term, and reads the exhortation as enforced from what was deemed prudent in ordinary lawsuits, where men should make up matters with the utmost speed, since running through the whole course of a suit must be vexatious and attended with great expense, and in the end, though the loser may be ruined, the gainer has nothing. A good use of this prudential advice he then makes, that the sinner, with whom God has a controversy and who is but a step from death, should come immediately at the call of Christ and be saved; but he adds a sharp warning, that those who make the adversary God, the judge Christ, the officer Death and the prison Hell abuse the passage and highly dishonour God. The farthing he traces through the rabbinical corruptions of the Greek word and the table of small coins, the smallest piece among the Jews weighing half a barley-corn; and he closes by refusing the passage to two doctrines: it has been considered a proper foundation on which to build not only the doctrine of a purgatory but also that of universal restoration, yet the most unwarrantable violence must be used before it can be pressed into the service of either of those unscriptural doctrines, the text being at most a metaphor. Wesley notes that they had heard the law from the scribes reciting it, and that they interpreted this as all the other commandments barely of the outward act; the judgment he identifies as the court of twenty-three in every city which could sentence a criminal to be strangled, while the great council at Jerusalem alone could sentence to the more terrible death of stoning. On the words but I say unto you he asks which of the prophets ever spake thus, their language being, thus saith the Lord, and who has authority to use this language but the one lawgiver who is able to save and to destroy. The clause without a cause he rejects on different ground from Clarke's: some copies add it, but this is utterly foreign to the whole scope and tenor of our Lord's discourse, for if he had only forbidden being angry without a cause there was no manner of need of that solemn declaration, since the scribes and Pharisees themselves said as much, even they teaching that men ought not to be angry without a cause, so that this righteousness would not exceed theirs; but Christ teaches that we ought not for any cause to be so angry as to call any man a fool, nor for any cause to be angry at the person. The brother's having aught against us he refers to any of the preceding accounts, any unkind thought or word, any that did not spring from love; and the leaving of the gift he explains by saying that neither the gift nor the prayer will atone for the want of love, but this will make them both an abomination before God. The last farthing he glosses briefly and absolutely, that is, for ever, since thou canst never do this.

Henry sets out the method: Christ having laid down the principles that Moses and the prophets were still to be their rulers but that the scribes and Pharisees were to be their rulers no longer, proceeds to expound the law in some particular instances and to vindicate it from the corrupt glosses which those expositors had put upon it, adding nothing new but limiting and restraining some permissions which had been abused, and as to the precepts showing the breadth and strictness and spiritual nature of them. The command itself he notes was delivered to them of old time, so that the laws of God are not novel upstart laws but ancient laws, of such a nature as never to be antiquated; killing is forbidden, killing ourselves, killing any other, directly or indirectly, or being any way accessory to it, the law of God being a hedge of protection about our lives. The exposition the Jewish teachers contented themselves with was that wilful murderers were liable to the sword of justice, and he finds that gloss faulty in two ways: it intimated that the law of the sixth commandment was only external and forbade no more than the act of murder, laying no restraint upon the inward lusts from which wars and fightings come, which he calls the fundamental error of the Jewish teachers, who were disposed to rest in the letter of the law and never enquired into its spiritual meaning; and it treated the law as merely political and municipal, given for them and intended as a directory for their courts and no more, as if they only were the people and the wisdom of the law must die with them. Christ's own exposition he takes in three parts. Rash anger is heart-murder, by our brother being meant any person though ever so much our inferior, since we are all made of one blood; anger is a natural passion and there are cases in which it is lawful and laudable, but it is sinful when we are angry without cause, and he glosses the Greek word as meaning without cause and without any good effect and without moderation, giving three heads: when it is without any just provocation given, as when we are angry at children or servants for what could not be helped, or upon groundless surmises, or for trivial affronts not worth speaking of; when it is without any good end aimed at, merely to show our authority or gratify a brutish passion, whereas if we are angry at all it should be to awaken the offender to repentance; and when it exceeds due bounds, when we are hardy and headstrong and violent and seek the hurt of those we are displeased at, for he that is thus angry would kill if he could and durst. Opprobrious language he calls tongue-murder, and distinguishes the two words: the first is a scornful word coming from pride, the language of what Solomon calls proud wrath, which tramples upon our brother; the second is a spiteful word coming from hatred, looking upon him not only as mean but as vile and abandoned of God, so that the more the reproach touches his spiritual condition the worse it is. Malicious slanders and censures he calls poison under the tongue that kills secretly and slowly, and bitter words arrows or a sword in the bones, whereby the good name of our neighbour, which is better than life, is stabbed and murdered. The three penalties he reads, following Whitby and others, in allusion to the penalties used in the several courts of judgment among the Jews, so that Christ shows the sin of rash anger exposing men to lower or higher punishments according to the degrees of its proceeding, and thus shows which sin is most sinful by showing which punishment is most dreadful. From all this he infers that we ought carefully to preserve Christian love and peace with our brethren, and that if a breach happens we should labour for reconciliation by confessing our fault, humbling ourselves, begging pardon and making restitution, and should do it quickly, for two reasons. First, because till this is done we are utterly unfit for communion with God in holy ordinances: when we are addressing ourselves to any religious exercise it is good to take that occasion of serious reflection and self-examination; religious exercises are not acceptable to God if performed when we are in wrath, since prayers made in wrath are written in gall; love is so much better than all burnt-offerings that God will have reconciliation made before the gift be offered, being content to stay for the gift rather than have it offered while we are engaged in a quarrel; and yet the quarrel can be no excuse for the omission of our duty, since we are to leave the gift before the altar lest having gone away we be tempted not to come again, for many give their variance with a neighbour as the reason why they do not come to church, and one sin will never excuse another but will rather double the guilt. Second, because till this is done we lie exposed to much danger, both temporal and spiritual. On the temporal side, if the offence we have done will bear an action in which considerable damages may be recovered, it is our wisdom and our duty to our family to prevent that by a humble submission and a just satisfaction, since it is in vain to contend with the law and many ruin their estates by an obstinate persisting in offences which a little yielding at first would have pacified; it is good to agree, for the law is costly. On the spiritual side he applies the whole to our reconciliation to God through Christ: the great God is an adversary to all sinners, a law-adversary who has a controversy with them and an action against them; it is our concern to agree with him, and our wisdom to do it quickly while we are in the way, for while we are alive we are in the way and after death it will be too late; those who continue in a state of enmity to God are continually exposed to the arrests of his justice; Christ is the Judge to whom impenitent sinners will be delivered, and he that was rejected as a Saviour cannot be escaped as a Judge; hell is the prison into which those will be cast who continue in that enmity; and damned sinners must remain in it to eternity, since they shall not depart till they have paid the uttermost farthing, and that will not be to the utmost ages of eternity, divine justice being for ever in the satisfying but never satisfied.

debates: Whether the words without a cause belong to the text, where Clarke reports them wanting in the Vatican manuscript and in many versions and fathers and judges them a marginal gloss that crept in, preferring to render the Greek vainly, Ellicott leaves the question open since they are absent from many of the best copies and may either have been inserted to soften a harsh teaching or have stood there first and been struck out as giving too wide a margin for vague excuses, Wesley rejects them on the different ground that the clause is utterly foreign to the scope of the discourse, since the scribes themselves taught that much and this righteousness would not then exceed theirs, while Henry and Barnes both build on the clause as genuine, Henry glossing it as without just provocation and without good end and beyond due bounds, and Barnes distinguishing the anger against sin that is lawful.

Who the adversary is, where Clarke warns that those who make the adversary God, the judge Christ, the officer Death and the prison Hell abuse the passage and highly dishonour God, Barnes agrees that there is no propriety in regarding God as the sinner's adversary here, Ellicott divides the figure and makes the judge clearly God and the officers those who execute his judgment while the adversary is the neighbour we have wronged, Henry takes the step the other two refuse and makes the great God a law-adversary with an action against sinners, and Calvin turns the passage another way again, as spoken to take away occasion for hatred by reproving the obstinacy of men too tenacious of their own rights.

Whether the uttermost farthing can ever be paid, where Ellicott raises the question without answering it, noting that within the figure the debt might be discharged and the prisoner freed, as Romanist divines have inferred, though in practice the sentence would be lifelong, Clarke replies that the most unwarrantable violence must be used before the text will serve either purgatory or universal restoration, and Henry with Wesley holds it never paid, Wesley glossing it as for ever since thou canst never do this and Henry saying that divine justice will be for ever in the satisfying but never satisfied.
outliers: Clarke adds his own opinion that murder is probably the only crime that should be punished with death, and doubts whether capital punishment inflicted for any other crime is not itself murder.

Ellicott cites the Talmudic rule that a man who remembers leaven left in his house should return and remove it before finishing the Passover, and applies what the scribes required of the leaven of bread to the leaven of malice.
themes: Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not kill; and whosoever shall kill shall be in danger of the judgment:

But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire.
Therefore if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee;
Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift.

Agree with thine adversary quickly, whiles thou art in the way with him; lest at any time the adversary deliver thee to the judge, and the judge deliver thee to the officer, and thou be cast into prison.
Verily I say unto thee, Thou shalt by no means come out thence, till thou hast paid the uttermost farthing.

27.pericope_label: Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery: But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart. And if thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not that thy whole body should be cast into hell. And if thy right hand offend thee, cut it off, and cast it from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not that thy whole body should be cast into hell. It hath been said, Whosoever shall put away his wife, let him give her a writing of divorcement: But I say unto you, That whosoever shall put away his wife, saving for the cause of fornication, causeth her to commit adultery: and whosoever shall marry her that is divorced committeth adultery.

schools.summary: Ellicott notes first that the phrase about them of old time is omitted in the best manuscripts here and was probably inserted for conformity with the earlier verse; the words are simply those of the divine commandment, but given as it was taught in the Rabbinic schools, in the narrowness of the letter and without any perception that here too the commandment was exceeding broad, and it is with that teaching that our Lord contrasts his own. The intent of the looking he says is more strongly marked in the Greek than in the English: it is not the passing glance, not even the momentary impulse of desire, but the continued gaze by which the impulse is deliberately cherished till it becomes a passion. The teaching he defends against a familiar disparagement: it has often been remarked, and by way of disparagement, that this noble and beautiful teaching is found elsewhere, but such disparagement is out of place, since by the mercy of God the Light that lightens every man has led men to recognise the truth thus asserted, and parallels may be found in Confucius and Seneca and Epictetus and even the Jewish Rabbis themselves, Juvenal closely expressing the general sentiment that whoever cherishes a guilty thought in his breast bears the guilt of the action. On the word rendered offend he is exact: the Greek verb means strictly to cause another to stumble or fall into a snare, and this was probably the sense in which the translators used the word, though it is doubtful whether it ever had that factitive sense in English outside the Authorised version, and the common use of the word gives so different a meaning that it cannot be regarded as a happy rendering; he traces the variations of the successive English versions, offend in Tyndale, hinder thee in Cranmer, cause thee to offend in the Geneva, scandalise in the Rhemish, and offend again in the Authorised, and judges the Geneva beyond doubt the best. The plucking out he says the bold severity of the phrase excludes from a literal interpretation, since the seat of the evil lies in the will and not in the organ of sense or action, and the removal of the instrument might leave the inward taint unpurified; what is meant is that any sense, when it ministers to sin, is an evil and not a good, the loss of which would be the truest gain. The repetition with the hand he finds has in part the emphasis of iteration but points also to a distinct danger, since not the senses only, through which we receive impressions, but the gifts and energies which issue in action may become temptations to evil, and in that case it were better to forfeit them, the true remedy being found in so directing the will that eye and hand may each do its work in obedience to the law of righteousness. On divorce he reports the better manuscripts giving but it was said, as though stating an implied objection to the previous teaching, men thinking they could avoid the sin of adultery by taking the easy course of divorcing one wife before marrying another; the quotation he says is given as the popular Rabbinic explanation of the Mosaic precept, which was given on account of the hardness of men's hearts to prevent yet greater evils. The words of the precept being vague, two schools of casuists took opposite views: the stricter party of Shammai held that the uncleanness meant simply unchastity before or after marriage, while the followers of Hillel held, as Milton among Christian teachers, that anything which made the company of the wife distasteful was a sufficient ground for repudiation, and even a moralist generally so pure and noble as the son of Sirach took the laxer view. The exception he takes to be expressed by the most generic term intentionally, so as to include ante-nuptial as well as post-nuptial sin, possibly indeed with reference to the former only, seeing that the strict letter of the Law of Moses made death the punishment of the latter and so excluded the possibility of the adultery of a second marriage. The words causing her to commit adultery he says imply that the putting away was legally a divorce from the bond, leaving the wife and still more the husband at liberty to marry again, for otherwise she could not have incurred the guilt of adultery by a second marriage; but the clause asserts that in such a case, when divorce was obtained on any other ground than the specific sin which violated the essence of the marriage contract, man's law, even that of Moses, was at variance with the true eternal law of God. Barnes says it is probable the Pharisees had explained this commandment as they had the sixth, as extending only to the external act, and regarded evil thoughts and a wanton imagination as of little consequence or as not forbidden by the law, whereas our Saviour assures them that the commandment did not regard the external act merely but the secrets of the heart and the movements of the eye, so that they who indulge a wanton desire have already in the sight of God violated the commandment; such was the guilt of David, whose deep and awful crime fully shows the danger of indulging in evil desires and in the rovings of a wanton eye. The right eye and hand he explains by the Hebrew habit of representing the affections of the mind by the members or parts of the body, the bowels denoting compassion, the heart affection or feeling, the reins understanding or secret purpose, and an evil eye sometimes envy and sometimes an evil passion or sin in general; here it is used to denote strong adulterous passion, unlawful desire and inclination, and the right eye and hand are mentioned because they are of most use to us, denoting that however strong the passion may be or difficult to part with, yet we should do it. The word offend he traces to a noun commonly meaning a stumbling-block, a stone placed in the way over which one might fall, or a net. On divorce he says the husband was directed, if he put his wife away, to give her a certificate of the fact that she had been his wife and that he had dissolved the marriage, and that there was considerable difference of opinion among the Jews for what causes he was permitted to do this, one famous school maintaining that it might be done for any cause however trivial and the other that adultery only could justify it; but the truth, he says, was that the husband exercised this right at pleasure, being judge in the case and dismissing his wife when and for what cause he chose, which seems agreeable to the law in Deuteronomy, while our Saviour says this was permitted on account of the hardness of their hearts and that in the beginning it was not so. Lightfoot shows that the text is cited not as barely delivered by Moses but as deformed by those of old time with a gloss that almost evacuated all the force of the command, since they interpreted it of the act of adultery only, and that with a married woman; and he quotes the enumeration of the precepts of the law, where this commandment is given as the rule that no man lie with another man's wife. He then sets the rabbinical sayings about looking beside the inconsistency of the rabbis' own practice, and on the hand he cites the tract which adjudges even the slightest handling to the cutting off of the hand, with the saying that it is better that a man's belly should be cleft in two than that he should descend into the well of corruption. On divorce he takes notice how our Saviour passes into the words by using the particle but, which has this emphasis in the place, that it whispers a silent objection which is answered in the following verse: Christ had said that whoever looks on a woman to lust after her has committed adultery already, but the Jewish lawyers said that if any one sees a woman he is delighted with above his wife, let him dismiss his wife and marry her. Among the chapters of Talmudical doctrine, Lightfoot adds, we meet with none treated more largely and more to a punctilio than divorces, and yet there the chief care is not so much for a just cause of it as for the manner and form of doing it. On the last verse he distinguishes three things: our Saviour does not abrogate Moses' permission of divorces but tolerates it, yet keeping it within the Mosaic bounds, that is, in the case of adultery, condemning the liberty of the Jewish canons which allowed it for any cause; divorce was not commanded in the case of adultery but permitted, since Israelites were sometimes compelled even by whipping to put away their wives, whereas our Saviour even in the case of adultery does not impose a compulsion to divorce but indulges a license to do it; and he that puts away his wife without the cause of fornication makes her commit adultery, that is, if she commits adultery, or although she commit it not in act, yet he is guilty of all the lustful motions of her that is put away, since he that lustfully desires is said to commit adultery. Robertson notes that the quotations from the Decalogue in this chapter are from the Septuagint and use the volitive future, a common Greek idiom, and compares the forms used in the other clauses. The heart he says is not just the centre of the blood circulation, though it means that, and not just the emotional part of man's nature, but here the inner man including the intellect, the affections and the will, the word being exceedingly common in the New Testament and from a root meaning to quiver or palpitate; Jesus locates adultery in the eye and heart before the outward act, and Robertson quotes two pertinent rabbinical sayings, that the eye and the heart are the two brokers of sin, and that passions lodge only in him who sees, whence he draws the peril of lewd pictures and plays to the pure. On the word for causing to stumble he says the rendering offend is far better given as ensnare, the notion being not that of giving offence or provoking but of setting a trap or snare for one, the substantive meaning the stick in the trap that springs and closes it when the animal touches it; the vivid pictures are not to be taken literally but powerfully plead for self-mastery, and he quotes Bengel to the effect that it is not mutilating of the body that Christ enjoins but control of the body against sin, adding that modern surgery finely illustrates the teaching, since the tonsils and the teeth and the appendix, to go no further, if left diseased will destroy the whole body. The writing of divorcement he identifies from the papyri, where the same phrase is used in commercial transactions as a bond of release, and observes that the written notice was a protection to the wife against an angry whim of the husband who might send her away with no paper to show for it. The exception clause he calls an unusual phrase that perhaps means except for a matter of unchastity, and reports that McNeile denies that Jesus made this exception because Mark and Luke do not give it, claiming that the early Christians made it to meet a pressing need; but Robertson fails to see the force of this charge against Matthew's report of the words of Jesus, and says it looks like criticism to meet modern needs.

Calvin says Christ proceeds with his subject and shows that the law of God has authority not only over the life, in a political view, to form the outward manners, but requires pure and holy affections of the heart; and he repeats what he has already stated, that though Christ quotes the very words of the law it is the gross and false meaning put upon it by dishonest interpreters that he blames, having already told us that he did not come as a new Legislator but as the faithful expounder of a law already given. It might be objected that through long practice that interpretation had grown old, and Christ expressly admits this but meets it by saying that the antiquity of an error ought not to be allowed to plead in its favour. The design, he says, was to condemn generally the lust of the flesh: not only those who have seduced their neighbours' wives but those who have polluted their eyes by an immodest look are adulterers before God. The mention of the eyes he calls a part put for the whole, since not the eyes only but even the concealed flames of the heart render men guilty of adultery, and Paul accordingly makes chastity consist both in body and in mind; but Christ reckoned it enough to refute the gross mistake which was prevalent, that it was only necessary to guard against outward adultery, and since it is generally by the wantonness of the eyes that temptations are presented to the mind, and lust enters as it were by that door, he used this mode of speaking when he wished to condemn lust. This teaches us also, Calvin adds, that not only those who form a deliberate purpose of fornication but those who admit any polluted thoughts are reckoned adulterers before God. On the plucking out he anticipates the complaint: it might be thought that considering the weakness of the flesh and of nature Christ pressed too severely on men, and the general meaning is that however difficult or severe or troublesome or harsh any commandment of God may be, no excuse ought to be pleaded on those grounds, because the justice of God ought to stand higher in our estimation than all that we reckon most precious. You have no right to object, he paraphrases, that you can scarcely turn your eyes in any direction without being suddenly drawn away by some temptation, for you ought rather to part with your eyes than to depart from the commandments of God. And yet Christ does not mean that we must mutilate our body in order to obey God; but as all would readily wish not to be restrained from the free use of their senses, he employs an exaggerated form of speech to show that whatever hinders us from yielding the obedience God requires in his law ought to be cut off, and he does so expressly because men allow themselves too much liberty in that respect. On divorce he defers the fuller treatment to its more suitable occasion and states briefly what Christ says here: as the Jews falsely imagined that they discharged their whole duty toward God when they kept the law in a national manner, so whatever the national law did not forbid they foolishly supposed to be lawful. Divorces which husbands were wont to give their wives had not been prohibited by Moses as to external order, but only, for the sake of restraining lewdness, he had ordered that a bill of divorcement should be given to the wives who were put away. It was a sort of testimonial of freedom, so that the woman was afterwards free from the yoke and power of the husband, while the husband at the same time acknowledged that he did not send her away on account of any crime but because she did not please him; and hence proceeded the error that there was nothing wrong in such putting away provided that the forms of law were observed. Since the bill bore that the woman had been loosed from her former husband and might enter into a new marriage, the man who unjustly and unlawfully abandons the wife whom God had given him is justly condemned for having prostituted his wife to others.

Clarke reports the opening phrase omitted by nearly a hundred manuscripts, some of them of the very greatest antiquity and authority, and by the Coptic, Ethiopic, Armenian, Gothic and Sclavonian versions, by four copies of the old Itala and by Origen and Cyril and Theophylact and Euthymius and Hilary, on which authority Wetstein and Griesbach have left it out of the text. The looking to lust after her he translates as earnestly to covet her, the verb being undoubtedly used here in the sense of coveting through the influence of impure desire, and he supports the sense from Herodotus and from a Latin commentator, saying that he dare not translate the passage he cites but that the learned reader will justify his rendering. In all these cases, he adds, our blessed Lord points out the spirituality of the law, a matter to which the Jews paid very little attention, since it is the property of a Pharisee to abstain only from the outward crime. The plucking out and cutting off he presses hard: we must shut our senses against dangerous objects to avoid the occasions of sin, and deprive ourselves of all that is most dear and profitable to us in order to save our souls, when we find that these dear and profitable things, however innocent in themselves, cause us to sin against God. Men often part with some members of the body at the discretion of a surgeon that they may preserve the trunk and die a little later, and yet they will not deprive themselves of a look or a touch or a small pleasure which endanger the eternal death of the soul; and it is not enough, he insists, to shut the eye or stop the hand, the one must be plucked out and the other cut off, and neither is this enough, we must cast them both from us, allowing not one moment's truce with an evil passion or a sinful appetite. On divorce he says the Jewish doctors gave great license in the matter, a man being allowed to divorce his wife if she displeased him even in the dressing of his victuals, and he quotes Rabbi Akiba, that if any man saw a woman handsomer than his own wife he might put his wife away because the law says, if she find not favour in his eyes, and the celebrated Jewish historian, who tells us in his own Life with the utmost coolness and indifference that about that time he put away his wife, who had borne him three children, not being pleased with her manners; these two cases, Clarke says, are sufficient to show to what a scandalous and criminal excess the matter was carried, though it was allowed by the school of Shammai that no man was to put away his wife unless for adultery, while the school of Hillel gave much greater license. The exception he will not render fornication: as that word signifies no more than the unlawful connection of unmarried persons, it cannot be used here with propriety when speaking of those who are married, and he therefore translates the phrase on account of whoredom. It does not appear, he adds, that there is any other case in which Jesus Christ admits of divorce, and a real Christian ought rather to beg of God the grace to bear patiently and quietly the imperfections of his wife than to think of the means of being parted from her; and to the objection that divorce was allowed by Moses he answers that it was permitted for the hardness of their hearts, but that what was permitted to an uncircumcised heart among the Jews should not serve for a rule to a heart in which the love of God has been shed abroad by the Holy Spirit, since those who form a matrimonial connection in the fear and love of God and under his direction will never need a divorce.

Henry calls this an exposition of the seventh commandment given by the same hand that made the law and therefore fittest to be its interpreter, the law against uncleanness fitly following the former, since that laid a restraint upon sinful passions and this upon sinful appetites, both of which ought always to be under the government of reason and conscience and are equally pernicious if indulged. The command includes a prohibition of all other acts of uncleanness and the desire of them, but the Pharisees in their exposition made it extend no further than the act of adultery, suggesting that if the iniquity was only regarded in the heart and went no further God could not hear it and would not regard it, and therefore they thought it enough to be able to say that they were no adulterers. Christ explains it in the strictness of it in three things which would seem new and strange to those always governed by the tradition of the elders. First, there is such a thing as heart-adultery, adulterous thoughts and dispositions which never proceed to the act; and the looking is not upon another man's wife only, as some would have it, but upon any woman. The command forbids all appetites to the sin, all lusting after the forbidden object, which is the beginning of the sin, lust conceiving, and where the lust is dwelt upon and approved and the wanton desire rolled under the tongue as a sweet morsel it is the commission of sin as far as the heart can do it, there wanting nothing but convenient opportunity. It forbids all approaches toward it, the feeding of the eye with the sight of the forbidden fruit, not only looking in order to lust but looking till I do lust, the eye being both the inlet and outlet of a great deal of wickedness of this kind, as the instances of Joseph's mistress and Samson and David witness; whence Henry asks what need we have, with holy Job, to make a covenant with our eyes, allowing them the pleasure of beholding the light of the sun and the works of God provided they never fasten upon anything that might occasion impure imaginations. The use of any other sense to stir up lust is likewise forbidden, and if ensnaring looks are forbidden fruit, much more unclean discourses and wanton dalliances, which he calls the fuel and bellows of this hellish fire; and he adds that those who dress and deck and expose themselves with design to be looked at and lusted after, like Jezebel who painted her face and tired her head and looked out at the window, are no less guilty, since men sin but devils tempt to sin. Second, such looks and dalliances are so dangerous and destructive to the soul that it is better to lose the eye and the hand that thus offend than to give way to the sin and perish eternally in it. Corrupt nature, he says, would soon object that it is impossible to be governed by such a rule, that flesh and blood cannot but look with pleasure, and such pretences will scarcely be overcome by reason and must therefore be argued against with the terrors of the Lord. The severe operation prescribed he states with care and then qualifies: if the right eye or the right hand cause thee to offend, and if it were indeed impossible, as is pretended, to govern them, and they have been so accustomed to these wicked practices that they will not be withheld, if there be no other way to restrain them, which, blessed be God, through his grace there is, it were better to pluck out the eye and cut off the hand, though the more honourable and useful, than to indulge them to the ruin of the soul; and if this must be submitted to, much more must we resolve to keep under the body, to live a life of mortification and self-denial, to keep constant watch over our own hearts and suppress the first rising of lust, to avoid the occasions of sin and decline the company of those who will be a snare to us though ever so pleasing, and to seek God's grace and depend upon it daily, which will be as effectual as cutting off a right hand. On the argument from hell he notes five things: that it is not unbecoming a minister of the gospel to preach of hell and damnation, nay he must do it, for Christ himself did it; that there are some sins from which we need to be saved with fear, particularly fleshly lusts, which are such natural brute beasts as cannot be checked but by being frightened; that when we are tempted to think it hard to deny ourselves we ought to consider how much harder it will be to lie for ever in the lake that burns with fire and brimstone; that in hell there will be torments for the body, the whole body being cast into hell, so that if we have a care of our own bodies we shall possess them in sanctification and honour; and that even those duties most unpleasant to flesh and blood are profitable for us, our Master requiring nothing but what he knows to be for our advantage. Third, divorcing wives upon dislike, or for any other cause except adultery, however tolerated and practised among the Jews, was a violation of the seventh commandment, as it opened a door to adultery. Henry is careful about the form of the old permission: Christ does not say here that it was said to them of old time, because this was not a precept, as those were, though the Pharisees were willing so to understand it, but only a permission, that whoever put away his wife should give her a bill of divorce, not thinking to do it by word of mouth when he is in a passion but deliberately, by a legal instrument in writing attested by witnesses, so that if he will dissolve the matrimonial bond he must do it solemnly. Thus the law had prevented rash and hasty divorces, and perhaps at first, when writing was not so common among the Jews, that made divorces rare things; but in process of time it became very common, and this direction how to do it when there was just cause was construed into a permission to do it for any cause. Christ, he says, reduced the ordinance of marriage to its primitive institution, that they two shall be one flesh, not to be easily separated, so that divorce is not to be allowed except in the case which breaks the marriage covenant; and he that puts away his wife upon any other pretence causes her to commit adultery, and him also that shall marry her when she is thus divorced, since those who lead others into temptation to sin, or leave them in it, or expose them to it, make themselves guilty of their sin and will be accountable for it.

debates: Whether the plucking out and cutting off are to be taken literally, where Ellicott says the bold severity of the phrase excludes a literal interpretation since the evil is seated in the will and not in the organ, so that removing the instrument might leave the inward taint unpurified, Calvin calls it an exaggerated form of speech and denies that Christ means we must mutilate the body, Robertson agrees that the vivid pictures are not to be taken literally but plead powerfully for self-mastery, quoting Bengel that it is control and not mutilation that is enjoined, while Clarke presses the other way, that it is not enough to shut the eye or stop the hand, the one must be plucked out and the other cut off and both cast from us, and Henry grants the severity but adds in a parenthesis that through grace there is another way to restrain them.

What ground of divorce the Mosaic precept allowed, where Ellicott names the two schools of casuistry, Shammai, who held the uncleanness of the precept to mean unchastity only, against Hillel, who held with Milton that anything making the wife's company distasteful was ground enough, Clarke supplies the instances of Akiba's saying and the historian's own cool notice of putting away the wife who had borne him three children, Lightfoot gives the lawyers' rule in the same terms and observes that the Talmud's care is for the manner and form rather than the just cause, and Barnes concludes that whatever the schools said the husband was judge in his own case and dismissed his wife when and for what cause he chose.

What the exception allows and whether it is authentic, where Clarke objects to the rendering fornication as improper of married persons and would translate on account of whoredom, Ellicott takes the generic term as chosen to include sin before marriage as well as after and reads the clause as setting man's law, even that of Moses, at variance with the eternal law of God, Lightfoot distinguishes that Christ tolerates the Mosaic permission within Mosaic bounds and even in the case of adultery indulges a liberty rather than imposing a compulsion, and Robertson reports and rejects McNeile's objection that the exception cannot be Christ's own since Mark and Luke omit it.
outliers: Robertson identifies the writing of divorcement from the papyri, where the same phrase serves in commercial transactions as a bond of release, and reads it as a protection to the wife against an angry whim of the husband.

Ellicott refuses to let the parallels in Confucius and Seneca and Epictetus disparage the teaching, since the Light that lightens every man has led others to recognise the same truth, and cites Juvenal's line to the same effect.
themes: Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery:
But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.
And if thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not that thy whole body should be cast into hell.
And if thy right hand offend thee, cut it off, and cast it from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not that thy whole body should be cast into hell.
It hath been said, Whosoever shall put away his wife, let him give her a writing of divorcement:
But I say unto you, That whosoever shall put away his wife, saving for the cause of fornication, causeth her to commit adultery: and whosoever shall marry her that is divorced committeth adultery.

33.pericope_label: Again, ye have heard that it hath been said by them of old time, Thou shalt not forswear thyself, but shalt perform unto the Lord thine oaths: But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God’s throne: Nor by the earth; for it is his footstool: neither by Jerusalem; for it is the city of the great King. Neither shalt thou swear by thy head, because thou canst not make one hair white or black. But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the quotation again as the letter of the Law as taught by the Rabbis, who did not go beyond it to its wider spirit: to them the third commandment was simply a prohibition of perjury, as the sixth was of murder and the seventh of adultery, and they did not see that the holy name might be profaned in other ways even when it was not uttered. They expressly or tacitly allowed many forms of oath in which it was not named, as with the view of guarding it from desecration; and then, out of the many forms thus sanctioned, they selected some as binding and others as not binding, and thus by a casuistry at once subtle, irrational and dishonest tampered with men's sense of truthfulness. On the sweeping prohibition he deals carefully with those who take it absolutely: not a few interpreters, and even whole Christian communities, as for example the Society of Friends, see here and in the Epistle of James a formal prohibition of all oaths, whether promissory or evidential, and look on the general practice of Christians and the formal teaching of the Church of England in her Articles as simply an acquiescence in evil. The first impression made by the words, he grants, is so strongly in their favour that the scruples of such men ought to be dealt with, as English legislation has at last dealt with them, with great tenderness. Their conclusion is nevertheless mistaken, he believes, on three grounds: because, were it true, our Lord would in this instance be directly repealing part of the moral law given by Moses instead of completing and expanding it as in the case of the sixth and seventh commandments, destroying and not fulfilling; because our Lord himself answered, when he had before been silent, to a solemn formal adjuration, and Paul repeatedly uses such forms of attestation; and because of the context. The oath by the head he takes as apparently chosen as an extreme instance of a common oath in which men found no reference to God, and observes that here too nothing but an implied reference to him fits it to be an oath at all, since he made us and not we ourselves, and the hairs of our head are not only numbered but subject in all their changes to his laws and not to our volition.
