On the last verse he notes that the translators seem to have preferred a somewhat pedantic Latin word for the more literal and homely English speech; the doubled yea he reports found in the Talmud and probably proverbial, and takes the sense to be that in all common speech a man's words should be as good as his oath, yes meaning yes and no meaning no even though there be no oath to strengthen it. The closing phrase he says may be either neuter, from evil in the abstract, or masculine, from the evil one, and with some hesitation, guided chiefly by the usage of a later chapter, he accepts the latter as the more probable: these devices of fantastic oaths come not from him who is the Truth but from him who, when he speaks a lie, speaks of his own. Barnes defines an oath as a solemn affirmation or declaration made with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed, imprecating his vengeance and renouncing his favour if what is affirmed is false; a false oath is perjury, or as here forswearing, and to perform unto the Lord is to perform literally and really and religiously what is promised in an oath. It appears, he says, from this passage as well as from the ancient writings of the Jewish Rabbins, that while they professedly adhered to the law they had introduced a number of oaths in common conversation which they by no means considered as binding, swearing by the temple, by the head, by heaven, by the earth; and so long as they kept from swearing by the name Jehovah, and so long as they observed the oaths publicly taken, they seemed to consider themselves safe. The prohibition he reads as limited to the manner which our Lord proceeds to specify, swearing not in any of the common and profane ways customary at that time. To swear by heaven, he says, was if it meant anything to swear by him that sitteth thereon, and swearing by the earth is really swearing by God; or perhaps the meaning is that we have no right to pledge or swear by what belongs to God, and that oaths by inanimate objects are unmeaning and wicked, since if they are real oaths they are by a living Being who has power to take vengeance. The footstool he glosses as that on which the feet rest when sitting, the term being applied to the earth to denote how lowly and humble an object it is compared with God; and Jerusalem is called the city of the great King because God was King of the Israelites and Jerusalem the capital of the nation and the place where he was peculiarly honoured as King. The oath by the head he says was common, and the Gentiles also used it; to swear by the head was the same as to swear by the life, or to say that one would forfeit one's life if what one said were not true, and since God is the Author of the life, to swear by that is the same as to swear by him; you have no control or right over your own life, you cannot even change one single hair, and it is therefore improper and profane to pledge what is God's gift and God's property. From the last verse Barnes draws two lessons of his own: that profane swearing is always the evidence of a depraved heart, since to trifle with the name of God or with any of his works is itself most decided proof of depravity; and that no man is believed any sooner in common conversation because he swears to a thing, since when we hear a man swear to a thing it is pretty good evidence that he knows what he is saying to be false, and he that will break the third commandment will not hesitate to break the ninth, which explains why profane swearers are seldom believed. Lightfoot states the fault of the old teaching exactly: the law forbids perjury, and to that the fathers of the traditions reduced the whole sin of swearing, little caring for a rash oath. In this chapter of oaths, he says, they doubly sinned, and the first count is that they were nothing at all solicitous about an oath so that what was sworn were not false, troubling themselves but little what or how or how often or how rashly you swear so long as what you swear be true. He sets out the fourfold distribution of oaths in the Talmudic tract and in Maimonides, beginning with the promissory oath, when a man swore that he would do or not do this or that, and the divisions of negative and affirmative oaths concerning something past and something to come. On the prohibition itself he quotes the rules prescribed to a religious man in another tract, among them that he be not too much in swearing and laughing, with the gloss of Rabbi Solomon that this means, be not much in oaths although one should swear concerning things that are true, for in much swearing it is impossible not to profane; and he concludes that our Saviour with good reason binds his followers with a straiter bond, permitting no place at all for a voluntary and arbitrary oath, so that the sense of these words goes in the middle way, between the Jew, who allowed some place for an arbitrary oath, and the Anabaptist, who allows none for a necessary one. The hair he glosses plainly, that a man can neither put on grey hairs nor lay them aside; and the doubled yea he gives in its Hebrew form, that business among the disciples of the wise men should be in truth and faith by saying yes, yes and no, no, adding the curious rule that if a lunatic is asked whether a bill of divorce shall be written for his wife and he nods, they try him thrice, and if he answers to no, no and to yes, yes, they write it and give it to his wife.

Calvin insists that this also is not a correction of the law but a true interpretation of it, for God condemned in the law not only acts of perjury but lightness in swearing, which lessens the reverence for his name; he does so who idly and contemptuously pronounces the name of God on trivial occasions or in ordinary conversation. While the law condemns every kind of profanation of the name of God, the Jews imagined that the guilt of it lay entirely in acts of perjury, and Christ reproves this gross error of supposing that they might without danger abuse the name of God provided they did not swear falsely. We are, no doubt, strictly enjoined to keep our oaths, since he who after employing the name of God cheats and deceives his neighbours does an injury to God as well as to man; but it is improper to confine to a single part that which has a wider reference. Some, he notes, consider the word as applying to vows, when anything has been promised to God on account of religion, but the mode of expression applies very well to all promises and engagements which have been sanctioned by the use of the name of God, for in such cases God is appealed to as guarantee between the parties to secure their fidelity. On the sweeping phrase he is at his sharpest. Many have been led by it to adopt the false notion that every kind of swearing is condemned by Christ; some good men have been driven to this extreme rigour by observing the unbridled licentiousness of swearing which prevailed in the world, and the Anabaptists too have blustered a great deal on the ground that Christ appears to give no liberty to swear on any occasion. But we need not go beyond the immediate context to obtain the exposition, for he immediately adds the particular forms, and who does not see that those kinds of swearing were added by way of exposition, to explain the former clause more fully by specifying a number of cases? The Jews had circuitous or indirect ways of swearing, and when they used them they reckoned it to be next to nothing, and, as one vice springs from another, they defended under this pretence any profanation of the name of God that was not openly avowed; to meet this crime our Lord declares that they must not swear either in this way or in that. Hence Calvin concludes that the particle relates not to the substance but to the form, and means neither directly nor indirectly; it would otherwise have been superfluous to enumerate those kinds, and therefore the Anabaptists betray not only a rage for controversy but gross ignorance when they obstinately press upon us a single word and pass over, with closed eyes, the whole scope of the passage. Is it objected that Christ permits no swearing? He replies that what the expounder of the law says must be viewed in connection with its design, and that the statement amounts to this, that there are other ways of taking the name of God in vain besides perjury. On the last verse he says Christ now prescribes a remedy, which is that men act towards each other sincerely and honestly, for then simplicity of speech will have quite as much weight as an oath has among those who are not sincere; and this is certainly the best way of correcting faults, to point out the sources from which they spring. Whence comes the great propensity to swearing, he asks, but from the great falsehood, the numerous impositions, the unsteady and light conduct, so that hardly anything is believed? Fairness and honesty in our words are therefore demanded by Christ, that there may be no longer any occasion for an oath, and the repetition means that we ought to abide by our words so that all may be convinced of our honesty; this is the true and lawful method of proceeding, when men have nothing on their tongue but what is in their heart. He then expressly rejects an exposition which others have given of the closing words, that the criminality of swearing ought to be charged on the man who does not give credit to what another says; Christ teaches us, in his opinion, that it originates in the wickedness of men that they are compelled to swear, for if honesty prevailed among men, if they were not inconsistent and hypocritical, they would maintain the simplicity which nature dictates. Gill holds that the prohibition must not be understood in the strictest sense, as though it was not lawful to take an oath upon any occasion, in an affair of moment, in a solemn serious manner and in the name of God, which may be safely done, but of rash swearing about trivial matters and by the creatures, as appears by what follows. That the Jews were wont to swear by the earth he says is clear from the instances, and it is condemned by Christ for this reason, because the earth is God's footstool, on which he treads and where he also manifests forth his glory, being a considerable part of the work of his hands; and swearing by the head he says was likewise a common form among them, of which he offers instances. On the doubled yea he explains that in common conversation and the daily business of life, when we answer to anything in the affirmative our speech should be yea and when in the negative nay, and for the stronger asseveration of the matter, when it is necessary, we should double these words, but let no oaths be joined to them, since this is enough, a righteous man's yea being yea and his no no, and his word sufficient. Hence it appears, he concludes, that our Lord is here speaking of rash swearing such as was used in common conversation, and justly condemns it; and he adds that the Jews have no reason to reject this advice of Christ, since they often use and recommend the same modes of expression themselves, endeavouring to raise the esteem of their doctors and wise men by saying that their words, both in doctrines and in dealings with men, are yea, yea.

Clarke says they dishonour the great God and break this commandment who use frequent oaths and imprecations even in reference to things that are true, and that those who make vows and promises which they either cannot perform or do not design to fulfil are not less criminal. Swearing in civil matters, he observes, has become so frequent that the dread and obligation of an oath are utterly lost in it; and in certain places where oaths are frequently administered people have been known to kiss their thumb or pen instead of the book, thinking thereby to avoid the sin of perjury, which he calls a shocking imposition on their own souls. The morality of the Jews on this point he pronounces truly execrable, since they maintained that a man might swear with his lips and annul it in the same moment in his heart, and he cites Rabbi Akiba as an example of this kind of swearing. On the oath by heaven he supplies a parallel from history, that it was a custom among the Scythians, when they wished to bind themselves in the most solemn manner, to swear by the king's throne, and that if the king was at any time sick they believed it was occasioned by someone having taken the oath falsely; and he asks who there is among the traders and people of this world who obey this law, adding that a common swearer is constantly perjuring himself and that such a person should never be trusted. When we make any promise contrary to the command of God, he says, taking as a pledge of our sincerity either God or something belonging to him, we engage what is not ours without the Master's consent; God manifests his glory in heaven as upon his throne, imprints the footsteps of his perfections upon the earth his footstool, and shows that his holiness and his grace reign in his temple as the place of his residence. The oath by the head he refuses for four plain reasons: God commands thee not to do it; thou hast nothing which is thy own, and shouldst not pledge another's property; it never did and never can answer any good purpose; and being a breach of the law of God it is the way to everlasting misery. The doubled yea he glosses as a positive affirmation or negation according to your knowledge of the matter concerning which you are called to testify: do not equivocate, mean what you assert, and adhere to your assertion; and he seals it with a line of Homer, that the man whose words agree not with his private thoughts is as detestable to him as the gates of hell. Whatever is more than a bare affirmation or negation, according to the requirements of eternal truth, he says is of the wicked one, that is the devil, the father of superfluities and lies, and he reports that one of Selden's manuscripts and Gregory of Nyssa, a commentator of the fourth century, read of the devil outright.

Henry takes this as an exposition of the third commandment, which we are the more concerned to understand aright because it is particularly said that God will not hold him guiltless, however he may hold himself, who breaks it by taking the name of the Lord in vain. It is agreed on all hands, he says, that the commandment forbids perjury and forswearing and the violation of oaths and vows, which is the true intent of the third commandment; perjury he calls a sin condemned by the light of nature as a complication of impiety toward God and injustice toward man, and so infallibly judged to be followed by the divine wrath that the forms of swearing were commonly turned into execrations, as when with us men say, so help me God, wishing they may never have any help from God if they swear falsely; thus by the consent of nations have men cursed themselves, not doubting that God would curse them if they lied against the truth when they solemnly called him to witness. The performing of oaths to the Lord he takes either of promises to which God is a party, vows made to God, which must be punctually paid, or of promises made to our brethren to which God was a witness, which must be performed to the Lord with an eye to him, since by ratifying a promise with an oath we have made ourselves debtors to him, and if we break it we have not lied unto men only but unto God. But the commandment, he adds, forbids not only false swearing but all rash and unnecessary swearing; not that all swearing is sinful, for so far from that, if rightly done it is a part of religious worship, and in it we give unto God the glory due to his name, and we find Paul confirming what he said by such solemnities when there was a necessity for it. In swearing, Henry explains, we pawn the truth of something known to confirm the truth of something doubtful or unknown, appealing to a greater knowledge and a higher court and imprecating the vengeance of a righteous Judge if we swear deceitfully. The mind of Christ in the matter he gives in five points. We must not swear at all but when we are duly called to it, and justice or charity to our brother or respect to the commonwealth makes it necessary for the end of strife, of which necessity the civil magistrate is ordinarily to be the judge; we may be sworn, but we must not swear, and may be adjured and so obliged to it, but must not thrust ourselves upon it for our own worldly advantage. We must not swear lightly and irreverently in common discourse, since it is a very great sin to make a ludicrous appeal to the glorious Majesty of heaven, a gross profanation of God's holy name which has no cloak and no excuse and is therefore a sign of a graceless heart. We must in a special manner avoid promissory oaths, of which Christ more particularly speaks here, since the influence of an affirmative oath ceases when we have faithfully discovered the whole truth, while a promissory oath binds so long, and may be broken so many ways by the surprise as well as the strength of a temptation, that it is not to be used but upon great necessity; and he adds that the frequent requiring and using of oaths is a reflection upon Christians, who should be of such acknowledged fidelity that their sober words should be as sacred as their solemn oaths. We must not swear by any other creature, and here Henry supposes there were some who, in civility as they thought to the name of God, would not make use of that in swearing but would swear by heaven or earth; Christ forbids this and shows that there is nothing we can swear by but it is some way or other related to God, who is the Fountain of all beings, so that it is as dangerous to swear by them as by God himself, since it is the verity of the creature that is laid at stake and that cannot be an instrument of testimony but as it has regard to God, who is the chief Truth. He then takes the four forms one by one: heaven is God's throne, where he resides and in a particular manner manifests his glory, so that you cannot swear by heaven but you swear by God himself; the earth is his footstool, which he governs as he rules in heaven, and which stands in relation to him as his, so that in swearing by it you swear by its Owner; Jerusalem the Jews had in such veneration that they could not speak of anything more sacred to swear by, but besides the common reference it has to God as part of the earth it is in special relation to him as the city of the great King; and the head, though near thee and an essential part of thee, is more God's than thine, for he made it and formed all its springs and powers, whereas thou canst not from any natural intrinsic influence change the colour of one hair, so that thou canst not swear by thy head but thou swearest by him who is the Life of thy head and the Lifter up of it. Therefore in all our communications we must content ourselves with yea and nay: in ordinary discourse, if we affirm a thing, let us only say, yea, it is so, and if need be, to evidence our assurance, we may double it; and if we deny a thing let it suffice to say no, or if requisite repeat the denial, for if our fidelity be known that will suffice to gain us credit, and if it be questioned, to back what we say with swearing and cursing is but to render it more suspicious, since they who can swallow a profane oath will not strain at a lie. It is a pity, he adds, that this which Christ puts in the mouths of all his disciples should be fastened as a name of reproach upon a sect faulty enough other ways, when, as Dr. Hammond says, we are not forbidden any more than yea and nay but are in a manner directed to the use of that. The reason given he thinks observable, that whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil, though it do not amount to the iniquity of an oath; an ancient copy, he reports, reads that it comes from the Devil, the evil one, and he adds that it comes from the corruption of men's nature, from passion and vehemence, from a reigning vanity in the mind and a contempt of sacred things, and from the deceitfulness which is in men, since all men are liars and therefore men use these protestations because they are distrustful one of another and think they cannot be believed without them. Christians should therefore, for the credit of their religion, avoid not only that which is in itself evil but that which comes of evil and has the appearance of it; an oath, he concludes, is physic, which supposes a disease.

debates: Whether the words swear not at all forbid every oath, where Ellicott grants that the first impression of the words favours those who think so, naming the Society of Friends and holding that such scruples deserve tender dealing, but judges the conclusion mistaken on three grounds, that Christ would then be repealing part of the moral law and destroying rather than fulfilling it, that he himself answered a solemn adjuration and Paul repeatedly used such forms of attestation, and that the context is against it; Calvin is less patient and calls it a false notion on which the Anabaptists have blustered, holding that the enumerated kinds were added by way of exposition so that the words relate not to the substance but to the form and mean neither directly nor indirectly; Lightfoot finds the middle way, that the sense goes between the Jew who allowed some place for an arbitrary oath and the Anabaptist who allows none for a necessary one; Gill says the words are not to be taken in the strictest sense, a solemn oath in an affair of moment being safely taken; and Henry agrees that swearing rightly done is a part of religious worship, making the magistrate the judge of the necessity, so that we may be sworn though we must not swear.

What the closing words cometh of evil mean, where Ellicott notes that the Greek may be either neuter, from evil in the abstract, or masculine, from the evil one, and with some hesitation accepts the latter, these fantastic oaths coming not from him who is the Truth but from him who speaks a lie of his own; Clarke reports that one of Selden's manuscripts and a fourth-century commentator read of the devil outright; Henry gives both senses, an ancient copy reading from the evil one while the thing itself comes from the corruption of men's nature and from the deceitfulness that makes men distrust one another; and Calvin rejects a third exposition altogether, that the criminality should be charged on the man who will not credit what another says, holding rather that it is men's own wickedness that compels them to swear.

What was wrong with the old teaching on oaths, where Lightfoot charges the fathers of the traditions with reducing the whole sin of swearing to perjury and caring little how often or how rashly a man swore so long as what he swore was true, Ellicott adds the second half of the mischief, that they allowed many forms in which the holy name was not uttered and then counted some binding and others not, by a casuistry at once subtle, irrational and dishonest, Barnes says that so long as they avoided the divine name and kept the oaths publicly taken they seemed to consider themselves safe, and Clarke calls the morality truly execrable since they held that a man might swear with his lips and annul it the same moment in his heart.
outliers: Clarke reports the Scythian custom of swearing by the king's throne in the most solemn manner, and the belief that if the king fell sick someone had taken the oath falsely.
Gill observes that the Jews have no reason to reject this counsel, since they themselves raise the esteem of their doctors by saying that their words, in doctrine and in dealing alike, are yea, yea.
themes: Again, ye have heard that it hath been said by them of old time, Thou shalt not forswear thyself, but shalt perform unto the Lord thine oaths:
But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God’s throne:
Nor by the earth; for it is his footstool: neither by Jerusalem; for it is the city of the great King.
Neither shalt thou swear by thy head, because thou canst not make one hair white or black.
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.

38.pericope_label: Ye have heard that it hath been said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth: But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also. And if any man will sue thee at the law, and take away thy coat, let him have thy cloke also. And whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain. Give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away.

schools.summary: Ellicott says the scribes here first took their stand on the letter, regardless of the aim and purpose of the Law, and then expanded it in a wrong direction. As originally given it was a check on the wild justice of revenge: it said, where the equilibrium of right had been disturbed by outrage, that the work of the judge was not to do more than restore the equilibrium, unless, as in the case of theft, some further penalty was necessary for the prevention of crime; it was, in its essence, a limit in both directions, not less than the eye for an eye, for that might lead to connivance in guilt, and not more, for that would open a fresh score of wrong. The scribes in their popular casuistry made the rule one not of judicial action only but of private retaliation, and it was thus made the sanction of the vindictive temper that forgives nothing. On the word for evil he says the Greek may be either masculine or neuter, and followed as it is by whosoever the former seems preferable, only here it is not the evil one with the emphasis of pre-eminence but the human evil-doer; of that mightier evil one, he adds, we are emphatically told that it is our duty to resist him. The smiting he notes was used of blows with the hand or with a stick, for which fines from a shekel upwards were imposed by Jewish courts. On turning the other cheek he puts the difficulty squarely: we all quote and admire the words as painting an ideal meekness, but most men feel also that they cannot act on them literally, and that to make the attempt, as has been done by some whom the world calls dreamers or fanatics, would throw society into confusion and make the meek the victims; the question therefore meets us whether they were meant to be obeyed in the letter, and if not, what they command. The lawsuit he finds the Greek putting more strongly, if a man is bent on going to law with thee, and takes it as another aspect of the same temper of forbearance: not in regard to acts of violence only but also in dealing with the petty litigation that disturbs so many men's peace, it is better to yield than to insist on rights, Paul giving the same counsel to the believers at Corinth, though here too the precept, absolutely binding as far as self-interest is concerned, may be traversed by higher considerations. The coat he identifies as the close-fitting tunic worn next the body and the cloke as the outer flowing mantle, the more costly garment of the two, and says the meaning of the illustration is obvious, that it is wise rather to surrender more than is demanded than to disturb the calm of our own spirit by wrangling and debate. The compelling he explains from the Persian postal system, the Greek word implying the special compulsion of forced service as courier or messenger under Government, organised on the plan of employing men thus impressed to convey Government dispatches from stage to stage; the use of the illustration here would seem to imply the adoption of the same system by the Roman Government under the empire, Roman soldiers and their horses being billeted on Jewish householders and others impressed for service of longer or shorter duration. The mile he notes shows the influence of Rome by the use of a slightly altered Latin word for the thousand paces which made up a Roman mile, a little short of an English statute mile; and he finds a like illustration of the temper that yields to such compulsion rather than struggle or resist in the teaching of the Stoic Epictetus, that should there be a forced service and a soldier lay hold on thee, thou shouldst let him work his will and neither resist nor murmur. The giving he calls another seeming paradox, our Lord enforcing a principle binding upon every one in the form of a rule which in its letter is binding upon no man: were we to give to all men what they ask we should in many cases be cursing and not blessing them with our gifts, and not so does our Father give us what we ask in prayer, nor did Christ grant the prayers of his disciples. What the words really teach as the ideal of the perfect life is the loving and giving temper that sees in every request made to us the expression of a want of some kind, which we are to consider as a call to thoughtful inquiry how best to meet the want, giving what is asked for if we honestly believe that it is really for the good of him who asks, and giving something else if that would seem to be better for him. Barnes notes that the command is found in three places in the law and that in those places it was given as a rule to regulate the decisions of judges, who were to take eye for eye and tooth for tooth and to inflict burning for a burning; as a judicial rule, he says, it is not unjust, and Christ finds no fault with the rule as applied to magistrates and does not take upon himself to repeal it. But instead of confining it to magistrates the Jews had extended it to private conduct and made it the rule by which to take revenge, considering themselves justified in inflicting the same injury on others that they had received; against this our Saviour remonstrates, declaring that the law had no reference to private revenge, that it was given only to regulate the magistrate, and that private conduct was to be regulated by different principles. The general principle Barnes states as not setting ourselves against an evil person who is injuring us, but even this general direction he says is not to be pressed too strictly, since Christ did not intend to teach that we are to see our families murdered, or to be murdered ourselves, rather than make resistance, the law of nature forbidding it. The compelling he explains from the Persian couriers at length: post-offices were then unknown, and in order that the royal commands might be delivered with safety and despatch in different parts of the empire, Cyrus stationed horsemen at proper intervals on all the great public highways, one of whom delivered the message to another so that intelligence was rapidly and safely communicated; these heralds were permitted to compel any person, or to press any horse or boat or ship or other vehicle that they might need, for the quick transmission of the king's commandments, and it is to this custom that our Saviour refers, so that rather than resist a public authority requiring your attendance and aid for a certain distance you should go peaceably twice the distance. The giving he calls the general rule, and holds it better to give sometimes to an undeserving person than to turn away one really necessitous, and good to be in the habit of giving; at the same time the rule must be interpreted so as to be consistent with our duty to our families and with other objects of justice and charity, and it is seldom, perhaps never, good to give to a man that is able to work, since to give to such is to encourage laziness and to support the idle at the expense of the industrious; if such a man is indeed hungry, feed him, and if he wants anything farther, give him employment, but if a widow or an orphan or a man of misfortune or a man infirm or lame or sick is at your door, never send them away empty. So of a poor and needy friend who wishes to borrow, we are not to turn away or deny him, though this too deserves limitation and must be done consistently with other duties, since to lend to every worthless man would be to throw away our property, encourage laziness and crime, and ruin our families, and of this every man is to be the judge. Lightfoot shows that the law is cited as clothed in the gloss of the scribes and as then received in the Jewish schools, where they resolved it not into a just retaliation but into a pecuniary compensation: if any cut off the hand or foot of his neighbour, they value this according to the example of selling a servant, computing at what price he would be sold before he was maimed and for how much less now he is maimed, and however much the price is diminished so much is to be paid to the maimed person; we have received by tradition, they said, that this is to be understood of pecuniary satisfaction, and where the law says that if a man cause a blemish in his neighbour the same shall be done to him, it means not that he should be maimed as he has maimed another but that when he deserves maiming he deserves to pay the damage. Against the Jewish doctrine Lightfoot sets the words of Christ, and quotes the tariffs: does any one give his neighbour a box on the ear, let him give him a shilling, or according to another authority a pound; does he give him a blow upon the cheek, let him give two hundred small coins, and if with the other hand, four hundred; and the same sum is set for twitching him by the ear or pulling off his hair or spitting so that the spittle falls upon him or taking away his coat, which Lightfoot bids us compare with the clause about the coat here. The coat he identifies from the Talmud as the talith, which the commentator explains as a cloak, and asks why it is so called, answering, because it is above all the garments, that is, because it is the outermost garment; in this upper garment were woven those fringes that were to put them in mind of the law, whence the saying that he who takes care of his skirts deserves a good coat, so that the disgrace was increased together with the wrong when that was taken away, concerning which they did not a little boast and in which they placed no small religion. The compelling he sets in the scheme of the five mulcts to be paid to one who had some corporeal wrong done him, according to the reason and quality of the wrong: a mulct for maiming if the party were maimed, a mulct for pain caused by the blow or wound, a mulct for the cure of it, a mulct for the reproach brought upon him, and a mulct for ceasing, when being wounded he kept his bed and could not follow his business; and he maps the clauses of our Saviour's words onto them, the first words about not resisting evil relating to the first, the smiting and the coat to the second and fourth, and the compelling to the last and the second. Robertson notes the preposition in the quotation with the notion of exchange or substitution, and says that like divorce this is a restriction upon unrestrained vengeance, quoting McNeile that it limited revenge by fixing an exact compensation for an injury; a money payment, he adds, is allowed in the Mishna, and the law of retaliation exists in Arabia today. On the evil he says the dative case is the same form for masculine and neuter, and lists the renderings of Weymouth and Moffatt and Goodspeed, observing that the examples will go with either view, since Jesus protested when smitten on the cheek and denounced the Pharisees and fought the devil always. The language of Jesus, he says, is bold and picturesque and is not to be pressed too literally, paradoxes startling us and making us think, and we are expected to fill in the other side of the picture; one thing certainly is meant, that personal revenge is taken out of our hands, and that applies to lynch-law, while aggressive or offensive war by nations is also condemned, but not necessarily defensive war or defence against robbery and murder, and he adds that professional pacifism may be mere cowardice. The coat he says is really a sort of shirt or undergarment and would be demanded at law, while a robber would seize first the outer garment or cloke, so that if one loses the undergarment at law the outer and more valuable one goes also. The compelling he explains from the same Persian system and notes that this very thing was done to Simon of Cyrene, who was thus compelled to carry the cross of Christ, the same verb being used. On the turning not away he quotes McNeile that this is one of the clearest instances of the necessity of accepting the spirit and not the letter of the Lord's commands, since not only does indiscriminate almsgiving do little but injury to society, but the words must embrace far more than almsgiving; and he recalls again that Jesus is a popular teacher who expects men to understand his paradoxes, adding that in the organised charities of modern life we are in danger of letting the milk of human kindness dry up.

Calvin says another error is corrected here. God had enjoined by his law that judges and magistrates should punish those who had done injuries by making them endure as much as they had inflicted, and the consequence was that every one seized on this as a pretext for taking private revenge, thinking that they did no wrong provided they were not the first to make the attack but only, when injured, returned like for like; Christ informs them, on the contrary, that though judges were entrusted with the defence of the community and invested with authority to restrain the wicked and repress their violence, yet it is the duty of every man to bear patiently the injuries which he receives. He then distinguishes two ways of resisting, the one by warding off injuries through inoffensive conduct, the other by retaliation; and though Christ does not permit his people to repel violence by violence, he does not forbid them to endeavour to avoid an unjust attack. The best interpreter of the passage, Calvin says, is Paul, who enjoins us rather to overcome evil by good than to contend with evil-doers; and we must attend to the contrast between the vice and the correction of it, since the present subject is retaliation and the manner of acting of those who render the like to those who have offended them, so that to restrain his disciples from that indulgence he forbids them to render evil for evil, afterwards extending the law of patience so far that we are not only to bear patiently the injuries we receive. The lawsuit he treats as another kind of annoyance, when wicked men torment us with suits, and Christ commands us even then to be so patient and submissive that when one garment has been taken we shall be prepared to give up the other. None but a fool, he insists, will stand upon the words so as to maintain that we must yield to our opponents what they demand before coming into a court of law, for such compliance would more strongly inflame the minds of wicked men to robbery and extortion, and we know that nothing was farther from the design of Christ; what is meant is the man who endeavours, on the ground of a legal claim and under pretence of proceeding by way of justice, to wrench from us a part of our property. If a man oppressed by an unjust decision loses what is his own, and yet is prepared, when it shall be found necessary, to part with the remainder, he deserves not less to be commended for patience than the man who allows himself to be twice robbed before coming into court; in short, when Christians meet with one who endeavours to wrench from them a part of their property, they ought to be prepared to lose the whole. Hence Calvin concludes that Christians are not entirely prohibited from engaging in lawsuits provided they have a just defence to offer, since though they do not surrender their goods as a prey they do not depart from this doctrine of Christ, which exhorts us to bear patiently. On the giving he compares the parallel: though the words related by Matthew appear to command us to give to all without discrimination, we gather a different meaning from Luke, who explains the whole matter more fully. First, it is certain that it was the design of Christ to make his disciples generous but not prodigals, and it would be a foolish prodigality to scatter at random what the Lord has given us; again, we see the rule which the Spirit lays down elsewhere for liberality. Let us therefore hold, he says, first that Christ exhorts his disciples to be liberal and generous, and next that the way of doing it is not to think that they have discharged their duty when they have aided a few persons, but to study to be kind to all and not to be weary of giving so long as they have the means. Christ affirms, moreover, that when in lending or doing other kind offices we look to the mutual reward we perform no part of our duty to God, and thus draws a distinction between charity and carnal friendship: ungodly men have no disinterested affection for each other but only a mercenary regard, so that, as Plato judiciously observes, every man draws on himself the affection which he entertains for others; but Christ demands from his own people disinterested beneficence, and bids them study to aid the poor from whom nothing can be expected in return.

Clarke refers the clause to the law of retaliation, which obliged the offender to suffer the same injury he had committed, and notes that the Greeks and Romans had the same law, so strictly attended to at Athens that if a man put out the eye of another who had but one, the offender was condemned to lose both his eyes, since the loss of one would not be an equivalent misfortune. It seems, he says, that the Jews had made this law, the execution of which belonged to the civil magistrate, a ground for authorizing private resentments and all the excesses committed by a vindictive spirit, revenge being often carried to the utmost extremity and more evil returned than had been received; and he adds that this is often the case among those who are called Christians. The evil he is fully persuaded ought to be translated the evil person, and our Lord's meaning is, do not repel one outrage by another, since he that does so makes himself precisely what the other is, a wicked person; and the turning of the other cheek means that rather than avenge thyself thou shouldst be ready to suffer patiently a repetition of the same injury, though he observes that these exhortations belong principally to those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake, who should leave the judgment of their cause to him for whose sake they suffer. The Jews, he says, always thought that every outrage should be resented, and thus the spirit of hatred and strife was fostered. On the lawsuit he says that everywhere our blessed Lord shows the utmost disapprobation of such litigations as tended to destroy brotherly kindness and charity, and that it is evident he would have his followers suffer rather the loss of all their property than have recourse to such modes of redress at so great a risk; having the mind averse from contentions, and preferring peace and concord to temporal advantages, is most solemnly recommended to all Christians, and we are great gainers when we lose only our money or other property and do not risk the loss of our souls by losing the love of God and man. The two garments he distinguishes the other way from the critics, making the coat the upper garment and the cloke the under, what we call the strait coat and the great coat. The compelling he traces to the Persian royal messengers or posts, who had the royal authority for pressing horses and ships and even men to assist them in the business on which they were employed, and he brings the custom down to his own day: these messengers are now termed chappars and serve to carry despatches between the court and the provinces, and when one sets out the master of the horse furnishes him with a single horse, and when that is weary he dismounts the first man he meets and takes his horse, there being no pardon for a traveller that refuses to let a chappar have his horse, nor for any other who should deny him the best horse in his stable. The giving and lending he calls a general precept from which we are only excused by our inability to perform it, men being more or less obliged to it as they are more or less able, as the want is more or less pressing, and as they are more or less burdened with the common poor or with necessitous relatives, in all which matters both prudence and charity must be consulted. That God, he adds, who makes use of the beggar's hand to ask our charity, is the same from whom we ourselves beg our daily bread, and dare we refuse him? Let us show at least mildness and compassion when we can do no more; and if we cannot or will not relieve a poor man, let us never give him an ill word nor an ill look, for if we do not relieve him we have no right to insult him. To give and to lend, he concludes, are two duties of charity which Christ joins together and sets on equal footing.

Henry says the law of retaliation is here expounded and in a manner repealed, and marks the form of the citation: the expression is only, ye have heard that it has been said, not as before concerning the commands of the decalogue that it was said by or to them of old time, for it was not a command that every one should of necessity require such satisfaction, but they might lawfully insist upon it if they pleased. In all the places where it is found it is appointed to be done by the magistrate, who bears not the sword in vain but is the minister of God, an avenger to execute wrath; it was a direction to the judges of the Jewish nation what punishment to inflict in case of maims, for terror to such as would do mischief and for a restraint to such as have mischief done to them, that they may not insist on a greater punishment than is proper, since it is not a life for an eye nor a limb for a tooth but a proportion to be observed; and it is intimated that the forfeiture in such a case might be redeemed with money, for when it is provided that no ransom shall be taken for the life of a murderer, it is supposed that for maims a pecuniary satisfaction was allowed. But some of the Jewish teachers, who he says were not the most compassionate men in the world, insisted upon it as necessary that such revenge should be taken even by private persons themselves, and that there was no room left for remission or the acceptance of satisfaction; and even now, when they were under the government of the Roman magistrates and the judicial law fell to the ground of course, they were still zealous for anything that looked harsh and severe. So far, he says, the rule is in force with us as a direction to magistrates to use the sword of justice according to the good and wholesome laws of the land, for the terror of evil-doers and the vindication of the oppressed, and as a rule to lawgivers to provide accordingly and wisely to apportion punishments to crimes. The New Testament precept, as to the complainant himself, is to forgive the injury as done to himself and no further to insist upon the punishment of it than is necessary to the public good, a precept consonant to the meekness of Christ and the gentleness of his yoke; and Christ teaches two things here. We must not be revengeful: the resisting of any ill attempt upon us is as generally and expressly forbidden as the resisting of the higher powers, and yet this does not repeal the law of self-preservation and the care we are to take of our families, for we may avoid evil and may resist it so far as is necessary to our own security, but we must not render evil for evil, nor bear a grudge, nor avenge ourselves, nor study to be even with those that have treated us unkindly, but must go beyond them by forgiving them. The law of retaliation, he says, must be made consistent with the law of love; nor, if any have injured us, is our recompence in our own hands but in the hands of God, to whose wrath we must give place, and sometimes in the hands of his viceregents where it is necessary for the preservation of the public peace; but it will not justify us in hurting our brother to say that he began, for it is the second blow that makes the quarrel. Three things he specifies as showing that Christians must patiently yield to those who bear hard upon them rather than contend. A blow on the cheek is an injury to me in my body, and not only a hurt but an affront and indignity; rather than avenge it, prepare for another and bear it patiently, give not the rude man as good as he brings, do not challenge him nor enter an action against him, and if it be necessary to the public peace that he be bound to his good behaviour leave that to the magistrate, but for thine own part it will ordinarily be the wisest course to pass it by, since there are no bones broken, and if proud fools laugh at thee for it all wise men will value and honour thee for it. The loss of a coat is a wrong to me in my estate, and he calls it a hard case, noting that it is common for legal processes to be made use of for the doing of greatest injuries, since though judges be just and circumspect it is possible for bad men who make no conscience of oaths and forgeries by course of law to force off the coat from a man's back; in such a case, rather than go to the law by way of revenge, rather than exhibit a cross bill or stand out to the utmost in defence of what is thy undoubted right, let him even take thy cloak also, for if the matter be small, which we may lose without considerable damage to our families, it is good to submit to it for peace' sake, since it will not cost so much to buy another cloak as it will cost by course of law to recover the first. The going a mile by constraint is a wrong to me in my liberty: grudge not at it, but go two miles rather than fall out with him, and say not, I would do it if I were not compelled to it but I hate to be forced, but rather, therefore I will do it, for otherwise there will be a quarrel, and it is better to serve him than to serve thy own lusts of pride and revenge. Henry reports another sense of it also, that the Jews taught that the disciples of the wise and the students of the law were not to be pressed as others might by the king's officers to travel upon the public service, but that Christ will not have his disciples insist upon this privilege, choosing rather to comply than to offend the government. The sum of all, he says, is that Christians must not be litigious: small injuries must be submitted to and no notice taken of them, and if the injury be such as requires us to seek reparation it must be for a good end and without thought of revenge; though we must not invite injuries, yet we must meet them cheerfully in the way of duty and make the best of them, and if any say that flesh and blood cannot pass by such an affront, let them remember that flesh and blood shall not inherit the kingdom of God. Second, we must be charitable and beneficent, not only doing no hurt to our neighbours but labouring to do them all the good we can: ready to give, looking upon the request of the poor as giving us an opportunity for the duty of almsgiving and giving at the first word when a real object of charity presents itself, yet guiding the affairs of our charity with discretion lest we give to the idle and unworthy what should be given to the necessitous; and ready to lend, which he says is sometimes as great a piece of charity as giving, since it not only relieves the present exigency but obliges the borrower to providence and industry and honesty. Be easy of access to him that would borrow, he urges, and shun not those whom thou knowest to have such a request to make, nor contrive excuses to shake them off, for though he be bashful and have not confidence to make known his case, thou knowest both his need and his desire and shouldst offer him the kindness; and he quotes the saying of Seneca, that he will be prevailed on before he is entreated and will anticipate the becoming petition, adding that it becomes us to be thus forward in acts of kindness, for before we call God hears us and prevents us with the blessings of his goodness.

debates: Whether the precept forbids resisting an evil person or an evil deed, and how far either is forbidden, where Clarke is fully persuaded that the Greek means the evil person and reads the sense as not repelling one outrage by another, Ellicott finds the word able to be masculine or neuter and prefers the masculine, not the evil one of pre-eminence but the human evil-doer, while remarking that of the mightier evil one we are expressly told it is our duty to resist him, Robertson leaves it open since the dative is the same for both genders and the examples go either way, and Henry and Barnes both guard the ground of self-preservation, Henry that the precept does not repeal the law of self-preservation or the care we owe our families and Barnes that Christ did not mean we should see our families murdered rather than resist, while Calvin distinguishes warding off injury through inoffensive conduct from retaliation and forbids only the second.

Whether the commands are to be obeyed in the letter, where Ellicott puts the question directly and observes that most men feel they cannot act on them so, and that the attempt by those the world calls dreamers or fanatics would throw society into confusion and make the meek the victims, while Robertson answers that the language is bold and picturesque and not to be pressed, that what is certainly meant is that personal revenge is taken out of our hands, which applies to lynch-law, and that defence against robbery and murder is allowed, adding that professional pacifism may be mere cowardice; Calvin keeps the lawsuit precept from absurdity, since none but a fool would make it mean that we must yield what is demanded before coming into court, and holds that Christians are not wholly forbidden lawsuits where they have a just defence.

Which garment is the coat and which the cloke, where Ellicott makes the coat the close-fitting tunic worn next the body and the cloke the outer flowing mantle, the more costly of the two, and Robertson agrees, the coat being a sort of shirt that would be demanded at law while a robber would seize the outer garment first, against which Clarke reverses them, making the coat the upper garment and the cloke the under, what we call the strait coat and the great coat, with Lightfoot supporting him from the Talmud, where the word is the talith, so called because it is above all the garments, the outermost, in which the fringes were woven that were to put a man in mind of the law.
outliers: Clarke notes that the Greeks and Romans had the same law of retaliation, so strictly observed at Athens that a man who put out the one eye of a man who had but one was condemned to lose both.

Ellicott finds a like illustration of the temper that yields to forced service in the Stoic Epictetus, that if a soldier lay hold on thee thou shouldst let him work his will and neither resist nor murmur.
