43.pericope_label: Ye have heard that it hath been said, Thou shalt love thy neighbour, and hate thine enemy. But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you; That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust. For if ye love them which love you, what reward have ye? do not even the publicans the same? And if ye salute your brethren only, what do ye more than others? do not even the publicans so? Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.

schools.summary: Ellicott says the latter clause was in form a Rabbinic addition to the former, and this is important as showing that our Lord deals throughout not with the Law as such but with the scribes' exposition of it. But it can hardly be said, he adds, that these words, as far as national enemies were concerned, were foreign to the spirit of the Law, since the Israelites were practically commanded to hate the Canaanites and Amalekites, whom they were commissioned to destroy; the fault of the scribes was that they stereotyped the Law, which was in its nature transitory, and extended it in a wrong direction by making it the plea for indulgence in private enmities. Our Lord cancels the Rabbinic gloss as regards national and still more private hatreds, and teaches us to strive after the ideal excellence which he realised, and to love, that is, to seek the good of those who have shown us the most bitter hostility. The words about doing good to them that hate you he reports omitted in so many of the most ancient manuscripts that most recent editors hold they were inserted in the fourth or fifth century so as to bring the verse into verbal agreement with Luke; taking the text as it stands, he notes the extension of the command to love our neighbour so that it includes even those whom natural impulse prompts us to hate, and the stress laid on prayer as the highest utterance of that love, since in such cases circumstances may preclude acts which would be rejected and words that would be met with scorn, but the prayer that they too may be delivered from the evil which has been their curse is always in our power, and in so praying we are drawing near to the mind of God and asking that our wills may be as his. The becoming children of God he renders more literally and with far fuller meaning as that ye may become: we cannot become like God in power or wisdom, the attempt at that likeness having been the cause of man's fall and leading evermore to a like issue, but we cannot err in striving to be like him in his love. And the love we are to reproduce, he is careful to say, is not primarily that of which the children of the kingdom are the direct objects, showing itself in pardon and adoption and spiritual blessings, but the beneficence which is seen in Nature, our Lord assuming that sunshine and rain and fruitful seasons are his Father's gifts and proofs, whatever may be urged to the contrary, of his loving purpose; and here again he finds the teaching of the higher Stoics presenting an almost verbal parallel, that if thou wouldst imitate the gods thou shouldst do good even to the unthankful, for the sun rises even on the wicked. The publicans he passes over briefly, remarking only that our Lord puts himself as it were on the level of those to whom he speaks: they despised the publicans as below them, almost as an outcast caste, and he speaks as if he were using their own familiar language yet with a widely different application, asking whether they were after all above the publicans if they confined their love to a reciprocity of good offices. The salutation he says gains a special vividness from the prominence of salutation in the social life of the East, since to utter the formal peace be with you and to follow that up by manifold compliments and wishes was to recognise those whom men saluted as friends and brothers; and he notes that the true reading here is heathen rather than publicans, so that the question becomes whether the followers of Christ were to be content with copying heathen customs. The final command he renders literally as ye therefore shall be perfect, the ideal future that implies an imperative, and prefers the better reading, your heavenly Father. The idea of perfection implied in the word, he says, is that of the attainment of the end or ideal completeness of our being; in us that attainment implies growth, and the word is used elsewhere of men of full age as contrasted with infants, while in God the perfection is not something attained but exists eternally, and we draw near to it and become partakers of the divine nature when we love as he loves. Barnes says the command to love our neighbour was a law of God, and that the inference that we must therefore hate our enemy was drawn from it by the Jews, who supposed that if we loved the one we must of course hate the other, being total strangers to that great peculiar law of religion which requires us to love both; a neighbour, he adds, is literally one that lives near to us, then one that is near to us by acts of kindness and friendship, which is its meaning here. On loving enemies he distinguishes two kinds of love involving the same general feeling, or springing from the same fountain of goodwill to all mankind, but differing so far as to admit of separation in idea: the one is that feeling by which we approve of the conduct of another, commonly called the love of complacency, the other that by which we wish well to the person of another though we cannot approve his conduct, which is the love of benevolence, and this love we are to bear towards our enemies. It is impossible, he says, to love the conduct of a man that curses and reviles us and injures our person or property, or that violates all the laws of God; but though we may hate his conduct and feel deeply that we are affected by it, we may still wish well to the person, pity his madness and folly, speak kindly of him and to him, and not return evil for evil. The sonship he explains through the word's variety of senses, Christians being called the sons or children of God as his offspring, as adopted, as his disciples and as imitators of him; and in this passage the word is used because in doing good to enemies they resemble God, who makes his sun to rise on the evil and the good and sends rain without distinction on the just and unjust, so that his people should show that they imitate him by doing good in a similar way. The reward he takes in the sense of deserving of praise: if you only love those that love you, you are selfish and not disinterested, it is not genuine love for the character but love for the benefit, and you deserve no commendation, since the very publicans would do the same. The publicans he describes as tax gatherers in a province of the Roman empire, where the Jews bore the foreign yoke with great impatience and paid their taxes with great reluctance, so that those appointed to collect them were objects of great detestation; they were besides men who would be supposed to execute their office at all hazards, men willing to engage in an odious and hated employment, often of abandoned characters, oppressive in their exactions and dissolute in their lives, and by the Jews they were associated in character with thieves and adulterers. The salutation he glosses as showing the customary tokens of civility, or treating with the common marks of friendship, which the worst men would do; Christians should do more, showing that they have a different spirit and treating their enemies as well as wicked men do their friends, both because it is right, being the only really amiable spirit, and because we should show that religion is not selfish and is superior to all other principles of action. The word perfect he says commonly means finished, complete, pure, holy, and was originally applied to a piece of mechanism, as a machine that is complete in its parts; applied to men it refers to completeness of parts, or perfection, when no part is defective or wanting. Thus Job is said to be perfect, that is, not holy as God or sinless, for fault is afterwards found with him, but his piety was proportionate, had a completeness of parts, was consistent and regular, and he exhibited his religion as a prince, a father, an individual and a benefactor of the poor, not merely a pious man in one place but uniformly; and this, Barnes says, is the meaning here, that we should not be religious merely in loving our friends and neighbours but should let our piety be shown in loving our enemies. Lightfoot says that here those poisonous canons might be produced whereby the people were trained up in eternal hatred against the Gentiles, and against Israelites themselves who did not in every respect walk with them in the same traditions and rites; and he gives one example in place of very many which are to be met with everywhere, concerning the Israelites who worship idols or who transgress to provoke God, and those who deny the law and the prophets, who are by precept to be slain if any can slay them, and that openly, but if not openly their death may be compassed secretly and by subtlety. And a little after, he notes with irony on the extreme charity of the Jews towards the Gentiles, that as to the Gentiles with whom they have no war, and likewise to the shepherds of smaller cattle and others of that sort, they do not so plot their death, but it is forbidden to deliver them. On the publicans he shows how odious they were to the Jewish nation, especially those sprung of that nation, and how they reckoned them the very worst of all mankind, which appears many ways in the evangelists and is the very same in their own writers: it is not lawful to use the riches of such men of whom it is presumed that they were thieves, and of whom it is presumed that all their wealth was gotten by rapine and all their business the business of extortioners, such as publicans and robbers are, nor is their money to be mingled with thine because it is presumed to have been gotten by rapine; among those who were neither fit to judge nor to give a testimony in judgment are numbered the collectors of taxes and the publicans; and publicans are joined with cut-throats and robbers.

Calvin thinks it astonishing that the scribes fell into so great an absurdity as to limit the word neighbour to benevolent persons, for nothing is more obvious or certain than that God, in speaking of our neighbours, includes the whole human race. Every man is devoted to himself, and whenever a regard to personal convenience occasions an interruption of acts of kindness there is a departure from that mutual intercourse which nature itself dictates; to keep up the exercise of brotherly love God assures us that all men are our brethren, because they are related to us by a common nature, so that whenever I see a man I must of necessity behold myself as in a mirror, for he is my own flesh. Now though the greater part of men break off in most instances from this holy society, yet their depravity does not violate the order of nature, for we ought to regard God as the author of the union. The single point of loving enemies he says includes the whole of the former doctrine, for he who shall bring his mind to love those who hate him will naturally refrain from all revenge, will patiently endure evils, and will be much more prone to assist the wretched; and Christ presents to us in a summary view the way and manner of fulfilling the precept, since no man will ever come to obey it till he shall have given up self-love, or rather denied himself, and till men, all of whom God has declared to be connected with him, shall be held by him in such estimation that he shall even proceed to love those by whom he is regarded with hatred. We learn from these words, he adds, how far believers ought to be removed from every kind of revenge, for they are not only forbidden to ask it from God but are commanded to banish and efface it from their minds completely. On the sonship he presses the command hard: when Christ expressly declares that no man will be a child of God unless he loves his enemies, who shall dare to say that we are not bound to observe this doctrine? The statement amounts to this, that whoever shall wish to be accounted a Christian must do it; and it is truly horrible and monstrous, Calvin says, that the world should have been covered with such thick darkness for three or four centuries as not to see that it is an express command, and that every one who neglects it is struck out of the number of the children of God. It ought to be observed, he cautions, that when the example of God is held out for our imitation this does not imply that it would be becoming in us to do whatever God does, since he frequently punishes the wicked and drives them out of the world, and in that respect he does not desire us to imitate him, for the judgment of the world, which is his prerogative, does not belong to us. The publicans he says Luke calls wicked and unprincipled men, not that the office is condemned in itself, for they were collectors of taxes, and as princes have a right to impose taxes so it is lawful to levy them from the people; but they are so called because men of this class are usually covetous and rapacious, nay deceitful and cruel, and because among the Jews they were the agents of a wicked tyranny. If any one shall conclude from the words of Christ that publicans are the basest of all men, Calvin says he will argue ill, for our Lord employs the ordinary phraseology, his meaning being that those who are nearly devoid of humanity have some appearance of discharging mutual duties when they see it to be for their own advantage. The final command he refuses to read as an equality: the perfection does not mean that there is an equality or the same measure, but relates solely to some resemblance or approach, and however distant we are from the perfection of God we are said to be perfect when we aim at the same object which he presents to us in himself. Or, should it be thought preferable, he offers another statement, that there is no comparison here made between God and us, but that the perfection of God means that free and pure kindness which is not induced by the expectation of gain, and that remarkable goodness which contends with the malice and ingratitude of men; and this appears more clearly, he says, from the words of Luke, for such kindness is there contrasted with a mercenary regard founded on private advantage.

Clarke reports a textual variant at the outset, that instead of the word for neighbour a manuscript of the eleventh century reads friend, so that the sense would be, thou shalt love thy friend and hate thine enemy; and this, he says, was certainly the meaning which the Jews put on it, for neighbour with them implied those of the Jewish race and all others were considered by them as natural enemies. Besides, he argues, it is evident that the Greek word among the Hellenistic Jews meant friend merely, Christ using it precisely in that sense in the parable where the question is asked which of the three was neighbour to him who fell among the thieves, the answer being he who showed him mercy, that is, he who acted the friendly part; the Hebrew word signifies friend, and the Greek translators render it by this word in more than a hundred places, while among the Greeks it was a very comprehensive term signifying every man, not even an enemy excepted. The Jews, he adds, thought themselves authorized to kill any Jew who apostatized, and though they could not do injury to the Gentiles in whose country they sojourned, they were bound to suffer them to perish if they saw them in danger of death. The command to love enemies he calls the most sublime piece of morality ever given to man, and meets the objection that it has appeared unreasonable and absurd to some: it is so because it is natural to man to avenge himself and plague those who plague him, and he will ever find abundant excuse in the repeated evils he receives from others, men being naturally hostile to each other. But Jesus Christ designs to make men happy, and he who hates another is necessarily miserable; our Lord prohibits that only which from its nature is opposed to man's happiness, and this is therefore one of the most reasonable precepts in the universe. But who can obey it, Clarke asks, and answers, none but he who has the mind of Christ; and if a man have it not, let him seek it from God, for it is that kingdom of heaven which Christ came to establish upon earth. This one precept, he says, is a sufficient proof of the holiness of the Gospel and of the truth of the Christian religion, since every false religion flatters man and accommodates itself to his pride and his passions, and none but God could have imposed a yoke so contrary to self-love, while nothing but the supreme eternal love can enable men to practise a precept so insupportable to corrupt nature. On the sonship he reports another variant, that instead of the word for children some manuscripts and the latter Persic version and several of the primitive fathers read like to, that ye may resemble your Father who is in heaven, which he says is certainly our Lord's meaning: as a man's child is called his because a partaker of his own nature, so a holy person is said to be a child of God because he is a partaker of the divine nature. There is nothing greater, he adds, than to imitate God in doing good to our enemies, and all the creatures of God pronounce the sentence of condemnation on the revengeful, a sentence written by the rays of the sun and with the drops of rain and indeed by all the natural good things the use of which God freely gives to his enemies; if God had not loved us while we were his enemies we could never have become his children, and we shall cease to be such as soon as we cease to imitate him. He who loves only his friends, Clarke says, does nothing for God's sake, and he who loves for the sake of pleasure or interest pays himself; God has no enemy which he hates but sin, and we should have no other. The publicans he explains from the Greek words for tax and farming, noting the two classes, the superior being Romans of the equestrian order and the inferior those mentioned in the Gospels, who it appears were mostly Jews, a class of men detestable among the Romans and the Greeks and the Jews for their intolerable rapacity and avarice, and abhorred in an especial manner by the Jews, to whom the Roman government was odious, since these in assisting to collect the Roman tribute were considered as betrayers of the liberties of their country; and he likens them to the tithe-farmers of certain college-livings in some counties of England, a principal cause of the public burdens and discontent. On the salutation he reports that instead of brethren upwards of a hundred manuscripts, several of them of great authority and antiquity, together with the Armenian and Slavonic and Gothic versions and the later Syriac and some of the primitive fathers, read friends; he scarcely knows which to prefer, and since brother is more conformable to the Jewish mode of address he would retain it in the text, though the other reading tends to confirm the variant he noted earlier. On the subject of giving and receiving salutations in Asiatic countries he refers to a collection of observations and discusses whether the word means embracing, as Doddridge supposed, or something of a much more general nature. The final command he makes very emphatic: God himself is the grand law, sole giver and only pattern of the perfection which he recommends to his children, and the words mean that ye shall be filled with the spirit of that God whose name is Mercy and whose nature is love. God has many imitators of his power and independence and justice, he observes, but few of his love and condescension and kindness, and he calls himself Love to teach us that in this consists that perfection, the attainment of which he has made both our duty and our privilege, for these words of our Lord include both a command and a promise. Can we be fully saved from sin in this world, Clarke asks, and calls it an important question to which this text gives a satisfactory answer: as in the infinite nature there is no sin but nothing except goodness and love, so in our finite nature there shall dwell no sin, for the law of the spirit of life in Christ Jesus shall make us free from the law of sin and death; God shall live in and fill and rule our hearts, and in what he fills and influences neither Satan nor sin can have any part. Wesley states the matter in a line, that God spoke the former part and the scribes added the latter. The blessing of enemies he glosses as speaking all the good you can to and of them who speak all evil to and of you, repaying love in thought and word and deed to those who hate you and showing it both in word and deed. The sonship he reads as continuance and manifestation, that ye may continue and appear such before men and angels; and the sunshine he takes as God giving the evil such blessings as they will receive at his hands, since spiritual blessings they will not receive. The publicans he describes as officers of the revenue, farmers or receivers of the public money, men employed by the Romans to gather the taxes and customs which they exacted of the nations they had conquered, generally odious for their extortion and oppression and reckoned by the Jews as the very scum of the earth. The salutation he turns upon the church: our Lord, he guesses, probably glances at those prejudices which different sects had against each other, and intimates that he would not have his followers imbibe that narrow spirit; and he exclaims, would to God this had been more attended to among the unhappy divisions and subdivisions into which his church has been crumbled, and that we might at least advance so far as cordially to embrace our brethren in Christ, of whatever party or denomination they are. The final command he reads as promise before precept: so the original runs, referring to all that holiness which is described in the foregoing verses, which our Lord in the beginning of the chapter recommends as happiness and in the close of it as perfection; and how wise and gracious is this, he says, to sum up and as it were seal all his commandments with a promise, even the proper promise of the Gospel, that he will put those laws in our minds and write them in our hearts. He well knew how ready our unbelief would be to cry out that this is impossible, and therefore stakes upon it all the power and truth and faithfulness of him to whom all things are possible.

Henry sets out how the law was corrupted by the comments of the Jewish teachers. God said, thou shalt love thy neighbour, and by neighbour they understood those only of their own country and nation and religion, and those only whom they were pleased to look upon as their friends; yet this was not the worst, for from the command to love their neighbour they were willing to infer what God never designed, that they should hate their enemy, and they looked upon whom they pleased as their enemies, thus making void the great command of God by their traditions, though there were express laws to the contrary, since they were told not to abhor an Edomite nor an Egyptian, though these nations had been as much enemies to Israel as any whatsoever. It was true, Henry grants, that God appointed them to destroy the seven devoted nations of Canaan and not to make leagues with them, but there was a particular reason for it, to make room for Israel and that they might not be snares to them; and it was very ill-natured to infer from that that they must hate all their enemies, though the moral philosophy of the heathen then allowed this, Cicero's rule being to injure no one unless previously injured. See, he says, how willing corrupt passions are to fetch countenance from the word of God and to take occasion by the commandment to justify themselves. The lesson Christ teaches instead he introduces by the speaker's own character, as the great Peace-Maker and general Reconciler who loved us when we were strangers and enemies; and he states the duty plainly, that though men are ever so bad themselves and carry it ever so basely towards us, that does not discharge us from the great debt we owe them of love to our kind. We cannot but find ourselves very prone to wish the hurt, or at least very coldly to desire the good, of those that hate us and have been abusive to us, but that which is at the bottom of this is a root of bitterness which must be plucked up, and a remnant of corrupt nature which grace must conquer. Henry is careful about the kind of love owed: we cannot have complacency in one that is openly wicked and profane, nor put confidence in one that we know to be deceitful, nor are we to love all alike, but we must pay respect to the human nature and so far honour all men, and must take notice with pleasure of that even in our enemies which is amiable and commendable, ingenuousness and good temper and learning and moral virtue and kindness to others, and love that, though they are our enemies, having compassion for them and good will toward them. He then gives three duties. We must speak well of them: when we speak to them we must answer their revilings with courteous and friendly words and not render railing for railing, and behind their backs we must commend what in them is commendable, for they in whose tongues is the law of kindness can give good words to those who give bad words to them. We must do well to them, which will be a better proof of love than good words, being ready to do them all the real kindness we can and glad of an opportunity to do it, in their bodies and estates and names and families, and especially to do good to their souls; and here Henry recalls that it was said of Archbishop Cranmer that the way to make him a friend was to do him an ill turn, so many did he serve who had disobliged him. And we must pray for them, since it is no new thing for the most excellent saints to be hated and cursed and persecuted and despitefully used by wicked people, Christ himself being so treated, and when we meet with such usage we have an opportunity of showing our conformity both to the precept and to the example of Christ by praying for them; if we cannot otherwise testify our love to them, yet this way we may without ostentation, and it is such a way as surely we durst not dissemble in, praying that God will forgive them, that they may never fare the worse for anything they have done against us, and that he would make them to be at peace with us, which is itself one way of making them so. Henry adds the saying of Aristo, that when one commended the reply of Cleomenes, who being asked what a good king should do said, good turns to his friends and evil to his enemies, he answered, how much better is it to do good to our friends and make friends of our enemies, which Henry calls the heaping of coals of fire on their heads. Two reasons he finds given to enforce the command. We must do it that we may be like God our Father, and he asks whether we can write a better copy, it being a copy in which love to the worst of enemies is reconciled to and consistent with infinite purity and holiness. From the sunshine and rain he draws six observations: that they are great blessings to the world and come from God, not of course or by chance; that common mercies must be valued as instances and proofs of the goodness of God, who in them shows himself a bountiful Benefactor to a world of mankind who would be very miserable without these favours and are utterly unworthy of the least of them; that these gifts of common providence are dispensed indifferently to good and evil, so that we cannot know love and hatred by what is before us but by what is within us, not by the shining of the sun on our heads but by the rising of the Sun of Righteousness in our hearts; that the worst of men partake of the comforts of this life in common with others, though they abuse them and fight against God with his own weapons, which is an amazing instance of God's patience and bounty, since it was but once that God forbade his sun to shine on the Egyptians when the Israelites had light in their dwellings, and he could make such a distinction every day; that the gifts of God's bounty to wicked men who are in rebellion against him teach us to do good to those that hate us, especially considering that though there is in us a carnal mind which is enmity to God yet we share in his bounty; and that those only will be accepted as the children of God who study to resemble him, particularly in his goodness. The second reason is that we may herein do more than others. Publicans love their friends, nature inclining them to it and interest directing them to it, and to do good to them who do good to us is a common piece of humanity of which even those whom the Jews hated and despised could give as good proofs as the best of them, since the publicans were men of no good fame yet grateful to such as had helped them to their places and courteous to those on whom they had a dependence; and shall we be no better than they? In doing this, Henry says, we serve ourselves and consult our own advantage, and what reward can we expect for that unless a regard to God and a sense of duty carry us further than our natural inclination and worldly interest? We must therefore love our enemies that we may exceed them, for if we must go beyond scribes and Pharisees, much more beyond publicans; Christianity, he says, is something more than humanity. It is a serious question which we should frequently put to ourselves, what do we more than others, what excelling thing do we do? We know more than others, talk more of the things of God than others, profess and have promised more than others, God has done more for us and therefore justly expects more from us, and the glory of God is more concerned in us than in others; but what do we more than others, and wherein do we live above the rate of the children of this world? In this especially we must do more, that while every one will render good for good we must render good for evil, which will speak a nobler principle and is consonant to a higher rule than the most of men act by; others salute their brethren and embrace those of their own party and way and opinion, but we must not so confine our respect. The closing exhortation he takes in two ways: in general, including all those things wherein we must be followers of God as dear children, since it is the duty of Christians to desire and aim at and press toward a perfection in grace and holiness and therein to conform themselves to the example of their heavenly Father; or in the particular before mentioned, of doing good to our enemies, since it is God's perfection to forgive injuries and to entertain strangers and to do good to the evil and unthankful, and it will be ours to be like him, we who owe so much, who owe our all, to the divine bounty, being bound to copy it out as well as we can.

debates: Whether the added clause about hating an enemy was foreign to the Law, where Wesley puts it in a line, that God spoke the former part and the scribes added the latter, Barnes calls the hatred an inference the Jews drew from the command to love, Calvin thinks it astonishing that they limited the word neighbour to benevolent persons when God in speaking of our neighbours includes the whole human race, and Henry holds the gloss flatly against the Law, which forbade them to abhor an Edomite or an Egyptian, and reads the commission against the devoted nations as a particular case to make room for Israel; but Ellicott will not go so far, holding that as to national enemies the words can hardly be called foreign to the spirit of the Law since Israel was practically commanded to hate the nations it was sent to destroy, the fault of the scribes being to stereotype a law transitory in its nature and then extend it to private enmities.

What kind of love is owed an enemy, where Barnes separates the love of complacency in another's conduct from the love of benevolence towards his person and assigns us the second, so that we may hate the conduct of a man who reviles us and still wish him well, Henry says the same and adds that we must pay respect to the human nature and take notice with pleasure of whatever in an enemy is amiable, Clarke calls the precept the most sublime piece of morality ever given to man and reasonable rather than absurd since he who hates another is necessarily miserable, holding that none but he who has the mind of Christ can keep it, and Ellicott marks the stress laid on prayer as the highest utterance of that love, since circumstances may preclude acts and words while prayer is always in our power.

What the closing command to be perfect means, where Barnes takes the word in its mechanical sense of a thing complete in its parts and instances Job, called perfect though fault is afterwards found with him, his piety being proportionate and consistent throughout, Ellicott reads the Greek as an ideal future implying an imperative and the perfection as the attainment of the end of our being, and Calvin denies any equality of measure, holding that the word relates solely to resemblance and that the perfection of God here means that free and pure kindness which is not induced by expectation of gain; against which Clarke takes the words as command and promise together and answers the question whether we can be fully saved from sin in this world by saying that as in the infinite nature there is nothing but goodness so in our finite nature no sin shall dwell, and Wesley reads it the same way, as the proper promise of the Gospel, on which God stakes all the faithfulness of him to whom all things are possible.
outliers: Clarke reports a manuscript reading friend for neighbour, and upwards of a hundred manuscripts reading friends for brethren in the salutation clause, each tending to confirm the other.

Wesley turns the salutation on the church, guessing that the glance is at the prejudices of rival sects, and wishing it had been better attended to among the unhappy divisions into which the church has been crumbled.
themes: Ye have heard that it hath been said, Thou shalt love thy neighbour, and hate thine enemy.
But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;
That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.
For if ye love them which love you, what reward have ye? do not even the publicans the same?
And if ye salute your brethren only, what do ye more than others? do not even the publicans so?
Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.
